notes.heading: Definitions examiners want in words
points: A set is a $\text{well-defined}$ collection of objects; 'well-defined' means you can always decide membership.
Roster form lists elements; set-builder form gives a rule: $\{x : x \in N,\ x < 10\}$.
$\emptyset$ has $0$ elements; $\{\emptyset\}$ has $1$ element (it contains the empty set).
$A \subseteq B$ means every element of $A$ is in $B$; $A \subset B$ is a proper subset.
Two sets are equal iff $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$ — this is the standard way to prove equality.

notes.heading: Subsets and the power set
points: A set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets in total, of which $2^n - 1$ are proper and $2^n - 1$ are non-empty.
Number of subsets containing a fixed element $= 2^{n-1}$; not containing it $= 2^{n-1}$.
Number of subsets of exactly $r$ elements $= \binom{n}{r}$; the power set is the union of all these.
If $n(A)=m$ and $n(B)=k$, then $n(A \cap B)$ lies between $\max(0, m+k-n(U))$ and $\min(m,k)$.

notes.heading: Cardinal-number formulas (the marks earners)
points: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$ — the base formula; rearrange for whichever quantity is asked.
$n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A)+n(B)+n(C) - n(A\cap B) - n(B\cap C) - n(C\cap A) + n(A\cap B\cap C)$.
For 'exactly two': $n(A\cap B)+n(B\cap C)+n(C\cap A) - 3n(A\cap B\cap C)$.
$n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B) = n(A \cup B) - n(B)$.

notes.heading: Real numbers and intervals
points: $N \subset Z \subset Q \subset R \subset C$ — sizes strictly increase, so $N \subset R$ is true.
Every real number is a complex number with imaginary part $0$; not every complex number is real.
Interval notation: $(a,b)$ open, $[a,b]$ closed, $[a,b)$ half-open.
$x \in (-\infty, 2]$ means $x \le 2$ — infinity never gets a square bracket.

notes.heading: Venn-diagram word problems — the 4-step drill
points: Step 1: label 'only A', 'only B' etc., placing $x$ in the triple overlap.
Step 2: convert every English statement into a set equation.
Step 3: use total = sum of parts; solve for $x$.
Step 4: check that no region is negative — that catches most errors.
Remember: $n(U)$ includes the 'neither' region.

notes.heading: JEE-level extras
points: Number of elements of $A \cap B \cap C$ can be found only from the total and the pairwise data using the three-set formula.
For sets of numbers: 'multiples of 3 less than 50' → $\lfloor 49/3 \rfloor = 16$ elements.
Union of intervals: solve each on the number line and merge overlapping intervals — never merge disjoint ones.

formulas.d: Total number of subsets of a set with n elements.
Proper subsets and non-empty subsets both equal 2ⁿ − 1.
Number of r-element subsets of an n-element set.

Things that are NOT in A; the 'neither' region in Venn problems.
Elements in exactly one of the two sets.
Number of ordered pairs; give the ordered pairs when asked.

traps: $\{\emptyset\}$ is not empty — it has one element, so $2^{1}=2$ subsets, not $1$.
$A \cap (B \cup C) = (A\cap B)\cup (A\cap C)$ — do NOT write $(A\cap B)\cup C$.
$n(A\cap B) \le \min(n(A),n(B))$: if a computed overlap exceeds this, your Venn equation is wrong.
Infinity is never bracketed: write $(-\infty, 5)$, never $[-\infty,5)$.
In 'exactly one of the papers' problems, add the three 'only' regions — not the union.
'At least one' $= n(A\cup B)$; 'none' $= n(U) - n(A\cup B)$.

notes.heading: Domain rules — the single most asked skill
points: Denominator: set $g(x) \ne 0$.
Even root: $\sqrt{g(x)}$ needs $g(x) \ge 0$; odd roots are fine for all reals.
Logarithm: $\log_a g(x)$ needs $g(x) > 0$ and base $a>0,\ a \ne 1$.
$\tan x$ needs $x \ne (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}$; $\cot x$ needs $x \ne n\pi$.
$\sin^{-1}g(x)$ needs $-1 \le g(x) \le 1$.
Take the intersection of all conditions — the domain is the common region.

notes.heading: Range by standard methods
points: Write $y = f(x)$, make it a quadratic in $x$, then use $D \ge 0$ — works for rational quadratic functions.
Use known ranges: $|x| \ge 0$, $x^2 \ge 0$, $e^x > 0$, $\sin x \in [-1,1]$.
For $\frac{a\sin x + b}{c\sin x + d}$ cross-multiply and bound $\sin x$.
$y = x + \frac{1}{x}$ for $x>0$ has range $[2,\infty)$; for $x<0$ it is $(-\infty,-2]$.

notes.heading: Types of relations (definition ⇒ test)
points: Reflexive: $(a,a) \in R$ for every $a$ in the set.
Symmetric: $(a,b) \in R \Rightarrow (b,a) \in R$.
Transitive: $(a,b),(b,c) \in R \Rightarrow (a,c) \in R$.
Equivalence = reflexive + symmetric + transitive (it partitions the set into classes).
Number of relations on a set of $n$ elements: $2^{n^2}$; reflexive: $2^{n^2-n}$; symmetric: $2^{n(n+1)/2}$.

notes.heading: Special functions at a glance
points: $|x| = x$ for $x \ge 0$ and $-x$ for $x<0$; always $\ge 0$.
$[x] \le x < [x]+1$; $[-2.3] = -3$ (floor, not truncation).
Fractional part $\{x\} = x - [x] \in [0,1)$.
$e^x$ and $\ln x$ are inverse functions: $\ln(e^x)=x$, $e^{\ln x}=x$.

notes.heading: Composition and inverse (Class 11 level)
points: $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$ — apply the inner function first.
$\text{Dom}(g\circ f)=\{x \in \text{Dom}f : f(x) \in \text{Dom}g\}$ — the trap in JEE questions.
Generally $f\circ g \ne g\circ f$.
$f^{-1}$ exists iff $f$ is one-one and onto; then $f^{-1}(y)=x \iff f(x)=y$.

notes.heading: Learn the table cold (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°)
points: $\sin$: $0,\ \frac12,\ \frac{1}{\sqrt2},\ \frac{\sqrt3}{2},\ 1$ — then write $\cos$ backwards.
$\tan = \sin/\cos$: $0, \frac{1}{\sqrt3}, 1, \sqrt3, \infty$.
$\sec, \cosec, \cot$ are reciprocals — never memorise them separately.

notes.heading: The identity toolkit
points: Pythagorean family: $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$, $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$, $1+\cot^2\theta=\text{cosec}^2\theta$.
$\cos 2A$ has three forms: $\cos^2A-\sin^2A = 1-2\sin^2A = 2\cos^2A-1$ — pick the one that fits the data.
When you see $1-\cos 2x$, immediately write $2\sin^2x$; when you see $1+\cos2x$, write $2\cos^2x$.
$\sin^2A = \frac{1-\cos2A}{2}$ and $\cos^2A = \frac{1+\cos2A}{2}$ — the power-reduction pair.

notes.heading: Transformations — product ⇄ sum
points: $2\sin A\cos B = \sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)$.
$2\cos A\cos B = \cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)$.
$2\sin A\sin B = \cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)$.
$\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\frac{C+D}{2}\cos\frac{C-D}{2}$; $\cos C+\cos D = 2\cos\frac{C+D}{2}\cos\frac{C-D}{2}$.
In triangle questions where $A+B+C=\pi$, convert everything into sines/cosines of $\frac{A+B}{2}=\frac{\pi-C}{2}$.

notes.heading: Conditional identities in a triangle
points: $\tan A + \tan B + \tan C = \tan A\tan B\tan C$ when $A+B+C=\pi$.
$\sin 2A+\sin 2B+\sin 2C = 4\sin A\sin B\sin C$.
$\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C = 1-2\cos A\cos B\cos C$.
$\cos A + \cos B + \cos C = 1 + 4\sin\frac{A}{2}\sin\frac{B}{2}\sin\frac{C}{2}$.

notes.heading: Maximum & minimum — two workhorses
points: $a\sin x + b\cos x$ has range $[-\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\ \sqrt{a^2+b^2}]$.
$\sin x \cdot \cos x = \frac12\sin 2x \in [-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$.
For $\sin\theta>0$: $\sin\theta + \frac{1}{\sin\theta} \ge 2$ by AM–GM; similarly for $\cos$ and $\sec$.
$\sin^2\theta + \text{cosec}^2\theta \ge 2$; $\tan^2+\cot^2 \ge 2$.

notes.heading: Graphs, periodicity & parity
points: $\sin x, \cos x$: period $2\pi$, range $[-1,1]$; $\tan x, \cot x$: period $\pi$.
$|\sin x|$ and $|\cos x|$ have period $\pi$; $\sin^2 x, \cos^2 x$ also period $\pi$.
$\sin$ is odd, $\cos$ is even — useful for integrals over $[-a,a]$.
Period of $\sin(kx)$ is $2\pi/|k|$; of $\tan(kx)$ is $\pi/|k|$.

formulas.d: Always convert to radians before calculus; keep degrees for geometry.
Watch the sign flip on the ∓.
Any product sin·cos becomes one sine.
Choose the form that matches the given data.
Cubic-in-cos equations reduce to triple-angle form.
Turns squares into first powers — essential in integrals.

When two ratios of different angles are added.
Sign is the trap — C−D in the second sine.

formulas.e: \tan A+\tan B+\tan C = \tan A\tan B\tan C \quad (A{+}B{+}C=\pi)

traps: Degree/radian mixing is the number-one silly error — $\sin 30 \ne \frac12$ (30 rad).
$\cos(A+B) = \cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B$: the middle sign flips for cosine, not for sine.
When you square an equation, check for extraneous roots by substitution.
$\tan A\tan B = 1$ means $A+B = \pi/2$ only if both angles are acute in context.
$\sin\theta > 0$ does not mean $\theta$ is acute — check the quadrant.
Range questions: $\sin\theta+\text{cosec}\,\theta \ge 2$ holds only for $\sin\theta>0$; for negative sine the sum is $\le -2$.

notes.heading: Complex-number arithmetic rules
points: Add/subtract like ordinary algebra, combining real and imaginary parts separately.
Multiply by expanding; use $i^2 = -1$ at the end.
For division multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
$\sqrt{-a} = i\sqrt{a}$ for $a>0$; be careful: $\sqrt{-1}\cdot\sqrt{-1} = -1$, not $+1$.

notes.heading: Modulus, conjugate and inequalities
points: $z\bar z = |z|^{2}$ turns division and simplification into real arithmetic.
Triangle inequality: $|z_1+z_2| \le |z_1|+|z_2|$; equality when the arguments are equal.
$|z_1+z_2|^{2} + |z_1-z_2|^{2} = 2(|z_1|^{2}+|z_2|^{2})$ — the parallelogram law, asked often.
If $|z|=1$ then $\bar z = 1/z$.

notes.heading: Argand plane geometry
points: $|z-z_0| = r$ is a circle of centre $z_0$, radius $r$; $|z-z_0|<r$ gives the interior.
$|z-z_1| = |z-z_2|$ is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining $z_1,z_2$.
$\arg\frac{z-z_1}{z-z_2} = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}$ gives a circle with the segment as diameter.
Distance between $z_1,z_2$ is $|z_1-z_2|$; the angle at $z$ in a triangle is $\arg\frac{z_1-z}{z_2-z}$.
Rotation about origin by $\theta$: multiply by $e^{i\theta}$.

notes.heading: Cube roots of unity — do not lose marks
points: $\omega = \frac{-1+i\sqrt3}{2},\ \omega^2 = \frac{-1-i\sqrt3}{2}$, and $\omega^3 = 1$.
$1+\omega+\omega^2 = 0$ ⇒ any polynomial in ω can be reduced to $a + b\omega$.
$\omega^{3n}=1$; reduce big powers modulo 3.
$a^3+b^3 = (a+b)(a+\omega b)(a+\omega^2 b)$ and $a^3-b^3=(a-b)(a-\omega b)(a-\omega^2 b)$ — the factorisation trick.

notes.heading: Quadratic equations — complete toolkit
points: Discriminant $D=b^{2}-4ac$: $D>0$ real distinct, $D=0$ equal, $D<0$ complex conjugate roots (when coefficients are real).
Sum $=\frac{-b}{a}$, product $=\frac{c}{a}$; useful for symmetric functions like $\alpha^{3}+\beta^{3} = S^{3}-3PS$.
Equation from roots: $x^{2}-Sx+P=0$.
Common-root condition: $\frac{c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}$ style elimination, or subtract the equations.
Sign of $ax^{2}+bx+c$: if $a>0$ and $D<0$ the expression is positive for all real $x$; for $a>0, D>0$ it is negative between the roots.

notes.heading: Inequalities & range using a quadratic
points: $ax^{2}+bx+c \ge 0$ for all $x$ ⇔ $a>0$ and $D \le 0$.
Minimum of $ax^{2}+bx+c$ ($a>0$) is $\frac{4ac-b^{2}}{4a}$ at $x=\frac{-b}{2a}$.
For range of a rational function, put $y=f_{\max}$ and demand real $x$, i.e. $D\ge 0$.
If roots are $\alpha<\beta$ then the expression takes the sign of $a$ outside and the opposite sign inside $(\alpha,\beta)$.

Multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments.
Take care to bring the answer into $(-\pi,\pi]$.

notes.heading: The two golden rules
points: You can add or subtract the same quantity on both sides without changing the inequality direction.
You can multiply by a $\text{positive}$ number without flipping; multiplying by a $\text{negative}$ number $\text{flips}$ the sign.
Taking reciprocals: if $0 < a < b$ then $\frac{1}{a} > \frac{1}{b}$; if $a < b < 0$ then $\frac{1}{a} > \frac{1}{b}$ as well; if $a < 0 < b$ the inequality direction is meaningless without splitting.
Squaring is $\text{not}$ an equivalence: $-3 < 2$ but $9 \not< 4$. Only square when both sides are known non-negative or use cases.

notes.heading: Solving linear inequalities
points: $ax + b > 0$ with $a>0$ gives $x > -b/a$; with $a<0$ it gives $x < -b/a$.

For fractional inequalities $\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} > 0$, bring everything to one side so one side is $0$, factor numerator and denominator, then make a sign chart — $\text{never cross-multiply}$ when the denominator contains $x$.
For $|x - a| < r$ the solution is $(a-r,\ a+r)$; for $|x - a| > r$ it is $(-\infty,\ a-r)\cup(a+r,\infty)$.
Double inequalities $a < f(x) < b$ are solved by splitting into two inequalities and taking the $\text{intersection}$ of the solution sets.

notes.heading: Graphical solution in two variables
points: The line $ax+by+c=0$ divides the plane into two half-planes; the inequality picks one side.
If the inequality is $\ge$ or $\le$, the boundary line is $\text{included}$ (solid); if it is $>$ or $<$, it is $\text{dashed}$.
Test with $(0,0)$ whenever the line does not pass through the origin; for lines through the origin pick $(1,0)$.
The solution of a $\text{system}$ is the $\text{intersection}$ of all half-planes, often a convex polygon (unbounded is allowed).

notes.heading: Modulus inequalities — JEE traps
points: $|x| < a \iff -a < x < a$ (when $a>0$).
$|x| > a \iff x < -a$ or $x > a$.
$|x-a|+|x-b|$ is piecewise linear with breakpoints at $a$ and $b$ — $\text{always draw the cases}$ on the number line.

notes.heading: Word problems & LPP preview
points: Translate every condition: 'at least' $\to \ge$, 'at most' $\to \le$, 'exceeds' $\to >$.
The feasible region's $\text{corner points}$ are where the optimum of a linear function will lie — this is the heart of Class 12 Linear Programming.
If the feasible region is $\emptyset$, the system has $\text{no solution}$.

formulas.d: If it satisfies, that side is the solution; otherwise the opposite side.

traps: Multiplying or dividing by a variable expression whose $\text{sign is unknown}$ without cases — $\text{always consider sign}$.
Cross-multiplying a fraction inequality when the denominator can be negative — $\text{bring to one side}$ and use sign chart instead.
Writing $|x| < -2$ as $-2 < x < 2$ — if $a<0$ then $|x|<a$ has $\text{no solution}$.
Forgetting to $\text{flip}$ the inequality when multiplying by a negative number.
For fractional $P(x)/Q(x) < 0$, the points where $Q(x)=0$ are $\text{not included}$ even if numerator zero makes it 0.

branches.title: JEE tricks
items: Rank of a word in dictionary order

notes.heading: When to multiply, when to add
points: If tasks happen $\text{together}$ (step 1 $\text{and}$ step 2), $\text{multiply}$ the counts.
If tasks are $\text{alternatives}$ (option A $\text{or}$ option B), $\text{add}$ the counts.
For 'arrange the letters of MISSISSIPPI' the repetitions force division by factorials of identical letters.
'At least one' problems are almost always faster via $\text{complement}$: total − none.

notes.heading: Permutations
points: $P(n,r) = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}$ — the number of ordered arrangements of $r$ distinct objects chosen from $n$.
With $\text{repetition allowed}$, each place has $n$ choices, so $n^{r}$.
$\text{Circular}$ arrangements of $n$ distinct objects around a round table: $(n-1)!$; if clockwise and anti-clockwise are same (necklace), divide by $2$.
Fixing an object in a specific position reduces the problem to $P(n-1,r-1)$.

notes.heading: Combinations
points: $C(n,r)=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$; this counts $\text{subsets}$, so order does not matter.
$C(n,r)=C(n,n-r)$ — choosing $r$ to include is the same as choosing $n-r$ to exclude.
Key identities: $C(n,0)=C(n,n)=1$, $C(n,1)=n$, and Pascal's rule $C(n,r)+C(n,r-1)=C(n+1,r)$.
For $\text{identical objects}$: the number of distinct permutations of $n$ objects where $p$ are of one kind, $q$ of another is $\frac{n!}{p!q!}$.

notes.heading: Restriction strategies
points: '$A$ and $B$ together': $\text{bundle}$ them as a block, count arrangements of blocks, then internal permutations.
'$A$ and $B$ never together': count $\text{all}$ minus $\text{together}$ (complement).
'$A$ and $B$ apart': arrange the $\text{others}$, create $\text{gaps}$, place $A,B$ in gaps.
'At most $k$': sum $C(n,0)+\cdots+C(n,k)$ or use complement if $k$ is large.

notes.heading: JEE special counts
points: Number of $\text{distinct words}$ from $n$ letters with repetitions: $n!/(p!q!\cdots)$.
Rank of a word: count words starting with each earlier letter in dictionary order, then recurse.
Derangements of $n$ objects (no object in its place): $!n = n!\left(1-\frac{1}{1!}+\frac{1}{2!}-\cdots+(-1)^{n}\frac{1}{n!}\right)$.
Number of $\text{functions}$ from $m$ to $n$ objects: $n^{m}$; $\text{one-one}$ functions: $P(n,m)$ if $n\ge m$.

formulas.d: Base; define 0! for formulas to work.
Ordered selections of r from n.
Each of the r places has n choices.
p identical of kind A, q of kind B, etc.
When restricted objects must stay apart.

traps: $P(n,r)$ vs $C(n,r)$: if $\text{order matters}$ (arrangements, words, numbers) use $P$; if $\text{order doesn't}$ (committees, teams) use $C$.
Circular arrangements: $\text{fix one person's position}$ to break rotation symmetry — don't divide by $n$ after using $(n-1)!$ again.
'At least' without complement leads to long casework and double counting.
For identical objects, $\text{divide}$ by factorials of repeats — forgetting this is the most common error.
'Number of ways to arrange' around a round table where $\text{flipping}$ gives same arrangement (necklace) needs $/2$; otherwise not.

notes.heading: Expansion and general term
points: $(a+b)^{n} = \sum_{r=0}^{n} C(n,r) a^{n-r} b^{r}$ for $n \in N$.
The $(r+1)$-th term is $T_{r+1}=C(n,r)a^{n-r}b^{r}$ — $\text{this is the workhorse for all 'find the coefficient' questions}$.
If $n$ is $\text{even}$, there is one middle term at $r=n/2$; if $n$ is $\text{odd}$, there are two middle terms at $r=(n-1)/2$ and $(n+1)/2$.
The $\text{constant term}$ in $(x + k/x)^{n}$ is the term where the power of $x$ is $0$ — set exponent $=0$ to find $r$.

notes.heading: Binomial coefficients
points: $C(n,r)=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$; also written $\binom{n}{r}$.
Pascal's identity: $C(n,r)+C(n,r-1)=C(n+1,r)$ builds the triangle.
Sum of all coefficients: $\sum_{r=0}^{n} C(n,r)=2^{n}$ (put $a=b=1$).
Sum of $\text{even-indexed}$ = sum of $\text{odd-indexed}$ = $2^{n-1}$ (put $a=1, b=-1$ and add/subtract).

notes.heading: Greatest term and greatest coefficient
points: To find the $\text{greatest term}$ in $(a+b)^{n}$ for positive $a,b$, examine $\frac{T_{r+1}}{T_{r}} = \frac{n-r+1}{r}\cdot\frac{b}{a}$ and find where it crosses $1$.
The $\text{greatest binomial coefficient}$ is $C(n, n/2)$ when $n$ even and $C(n,(n\pm1)/2)$ when $n$ odd.
For $(1+x)^{n}$ with $x>0$, the greatest term occurs around $r = \frac{(n+1)x}{1+x}$.
$\text{Independent term}$ questions are just $T_{r+1}$ with power of $x$ set to $0$.

notes.heading: Useful tricks
points: Approximation: for small $|x|$, $(1+x)^{n} \approx 1+nx$.
Remainder: $a^{n}+b^{n}$ expansions help in $\text{divisibility}$ problems.
Coefficient of $x^{k}$ in $(1+x)^{m}(1+x)^{n} = (1+x)^{m+n}$ gives Vandermonde's identity.
For $(x - 1/x)^{n}$ constant term exists only when $n$ is $\text{even}$.

formulas.d: For n in N; n+1 terms.
Use to find any coefficient or term.

traps: $T_{r+1}$ not $T_r$ — the $+1$ shift is the classic off-by-one error.
In $(x + a/x)^n$, the $\text{power of x}$ is $n-2r$ for equal powers; recompute when powers differ.
Greatest $\text{term}$ depends on $a,b,x$ values; greatest $\text{coefficient}$ is purely $C(n, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor)$.
Signs in $(a-b)^n$: $T_{r+1}$ has $(-1)^r$ — $\text{don't drop it}$.
Constant term exists only when the $x$-exponent equation has an $\text{integer}$ solution for $r$ between $0$ and $n$.

modules.title: Sequences & Series

branches.title: HP (harmonic)
items: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM equality when a=b
No direct formula for sum of HP

notes.heading: AP — know it cold
points: General term: $a_{n}=a+(n-1)d$; $n$-th term from the end equals $l-(n-1)d$ where $l$ is the last term.
Sum: $S_{n}=\frac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d] = \frac{n}{2}(a+l)$ when $l$ is the last term.
Arithmetic mean of $a$ and $b$: $AM=\frac{a+b}{2}$; if $a, A, b$ are in AP then $A=\frac{a+b}{2}$.
If three numbers are in AP you can set them as $a-d,\ a,\ a+d$ to exploit symmetry.
Common AP trap: 'the $p$-th term is $q$ and the $q$-th term is $p$' ⇒ $d=-1$ and sum $S_{p+q}=\frac{p+q}{2}(p+q+1)$ style.

notes.heading: GP — the geometric engine
points: General term: $a_{n}=ar^{n-1}$.
Finite sum: $S_{n}=\frac{a(1-r^{n})}{1-r}$ for $r\ne1$; if $r=1$ then $S_{n}=na$.
$\text{Infinite}$ GP sum exists only when $|r|<1$: $S_{\infty}=\frac{a}{1-r}$.
Geometric mean of $a$ and $b$ (positive): $GM=\sqrt{ab}$; if $a,G,b$ are in GP then $G^{2}=ab$.
For $\text{three numbers in GP}$ set them as $a/r,\ a,\ ar$; if product is given this cancels $r$.

notes.heading: AM, GM, HM inequality
points: For $a,b>0$: $AM=\frac{a+b}{2}$, $GM=\sqrt{ab}$, $HM=\frac{2ab}{a+b}$.
$AM \ge GM \ge HM$ with equality iff $a=b$ — $\text{the most quoted inequality in JEE}$.
For $n$ positive numbers, $AM \ge GM$ similarly.
If $AM$ and $GM$ of two numbers are $A$ and $G$, the numbers are the roots of $x^{2}-2Ax+G^{2}=0$.

notes.heading: Special sums and telescoping
points: $\text{Telescoping}$: write $T_{k}=f(k)-f(k+1)$ so the sum collapses to $f(1)-f(n+1)$.
Common telescoping form: $\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{k+1}$.
$\text{Arithmetico-geometric}$: $S=\sum (a+(k-1)d)r^{k-1}$ is summed by multiplying by $r$ and subtracting.

notes.heading: Choosing AP vs GP
points: If $\text{differences}$ are constant → AP; if $\text{ratios}$ are constant → GP.
Logs convert GP to AP: if $a,b,c$ are in GP then $\log a, \log b, \log c$ are in AP (for $a,b,c>0$).
If $a,b,c$ are in AP and $x,y,z$ are in GP with same pattern, look for substitution.

formulas.d: Single AM between a and b.
Set three in AP to simplify.

traps: $S_n$ is $\text{sum to n terms}$, not the $n$-th term — $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$.
Infinite GP sum $\frac{a}{1-r}$ is valid only for $|r|<1$; for $|r|\ge1$ the series $\text{diverges}$.
$GM=\sqrt{ab}$ needs $a,b>0$ (or both negative with care); for general $a,b$ the GM may not be real.
When asked for 'the $n$-th term from the end', use $l-(n-1)d$, not $a+(n-1)d$.
In telescoping, check $\text{indices}$ carefully: $\sum_{k=1}^{n} (1/k - 1/(k+1)) = 1 - 1/(n+1)$, not $1-1/n$.

modules.title: Straight Lines

branches.title: Forms of a line
items: Normal: x cosα + y sinα = p

branches.title: Pair of lines (JEE)
items: Homogeneous second-degree ax²+2hxy+by²=0 gives two lines through origin

notes.heading: Master the forms
points: $\text{Slope-intercept}$: $y=mx+c$ ($m=\tan\theta$, $c$=y-intercept).
$\text{Point-slope}$: $y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1})$.
$\text{Intercept form}$: $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1$ ($a,b$ are $x,y$ intercepts).
$\text{Normal form}$: $x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha=p$ ($p$ is perpendicular distance from origin, $\alpha$ the angle of that perpendicular).
$\text{General form}$: $Ax+By+C=0$ with slope $-A/B$ (when $B\ne0$).

notes.heading: Slope and angles
points: Slope $m=\tan\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle with the positive $x$-axis.
Two lines are $\text{parallel}$ iff $m_{1}=m_{2}$ (or both vertical).
Two lines are $\text{perpendicular}$ iff $m_{1}m_{2}=-1$ (or one horizontal, one vertical).
Acute angle $\theta$ between lines with slopes $m_{1},m_{2}$: $\tan\theta = \left|\frac{m_{1}-m_{2}}{1+m_{1}m_{2}}\right|$.
If $m_{1}m_{2}=-1$ the formula gives $\tan\theta = \infty$, i.e. $\theta=90°$.

notes.heading: Distance and foot
points: Distance from $(x_{0},y_{0})$ to $Ax+By+C=0$: $d=\frac{|Ax_{0}+By_{0}+C|}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}}$.
Distance between $\text{parallel}$ lines $Ax+By+C_{1}=0$ and $Ax+By+C_{2}=0$: $d=\frac{|C_{1}-C_{2}|}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}}$.
$\text{Foot}$ of perpendicular from $(x_{0},y_{0})$ to the line: $\frac{x-x_{0}}{A}=\frac{y-y_{0}}{B}=\frac{-(Ax_{0}+By_{0}+C)}{A^{2}+B^{2}}$.
$\text{Image}$ (reflection) of the point: $\frac{x-x_{0}}{A}=\frac{y-y_{0}}{B}=\frac{-2(Ax_{0}+By_{0}+C)}{A^{2}+B^{2}}$.
Side test: $Ax_{0}+By_{0}+C$ has opposite signs for points on $\text{opposite sides}$ of the line.

notes.heading: Family and concurrency
points: Family through intersection of $L_{1}=0$ and $L_{2}=0$: $L_{1}+\lambda L_{2}=0$.
Three lines are $\text{concurrent}$ iff $\begin{vmatrix} A_{1} & B_{1} & C_{1} \\ A_{2} & B_{2} & C_{2} \\ A_{3} & B_{3} & C_{3}\end{vmatrix}=0$.
To find the line through the intersection and parallel/perpendicular to another, write $L_{1}+\lambda L_{2}=0$ and impose slope condition to find $\lambda$.

notes.heading: Pair of straight lines (JEE extra)
points: $ax^{2}+2hxy+by^{2}=0$ represents two lines through the origin; they are real iff $h^{2}\ge ab$.
Angle between them: $\tan\theta=\frac{2\sqrt{h^{2}-ab}}{|a+b|}$.
They are perpendicular iff $a+b=0$ and coincident iff $h^{2}=ab$.
General second-degree $ax^{2}+2hxy+by^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0$ represents a pair of lines iff its $3\times3$ determinant $\Delta=0$.

formulas.d: Intercepts a on x, b on y.
One horizontal, one vertical is also ⊥.
Mirror image of point in line.
All lines through intersection of L₁,L₂.

traps: Slope formula needs $\Delta y / \Delta x$; $\text{vertical lines}$ have $\text{no slope}$ (undefined) — never write $m=\infty$.
In distance between $\text{parallel lines}$, first make $A,B$ $\text{identical}$ (multiply one equation) before using $|C_1-C_2|/\sqrt{A^2+B^2}$.
Foot/image formulas have $A,B$ in $\text{denominator}$ as $A^2+B^2$ — don't swap with something else.
Family $L_1+\lambda L_2=0$ misses $L_2$ itself when written that way; if $L_2$ is the answer, swap roles.
For angle between lines, $\tan\theta$ formula gives $\text{acute}$ angle; obtuse is $180°-\theta$.

modules.title: Conic Sections

branches.title: General & eccentricity
items: e=0 circle, 0<e<1 ellipse, e=1 parabola, e>1 hyperbola

notes.heading: Eccentricity — one number classifies everything
points: A $\text{conic}$ is the locus of a point whose distance from a fixed point (focus) is $e$ times its distance from a fixed line (directrix).
$e=0$: circle; $0<e<1$: ellipse; $e=1$: parabola; $e>1$: hyperbola.
Cutting a $\text{double cone}$: parallel to side → parabola; oblique → ellipse; parallel to axis → hyperbola; perpendicular to axis → circle.

notes.heading: Circle — centre and radius
points: Standard: $(x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}$; centre $(h,k)$, radius $r$.
General: $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0$ with centre $(-g,-f)$ and $r=\sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}-c}$ — real circle needs $g^{2}+f^{2}>c$.
$\text{Parametric}$: $x=h+r\cos\theta,\ y=k+r\sin\theta$.
Equation of tangent at $(x_{1},y_{1})$ on the circle (use $T=0$): $xx_{1}+yy_{1}+g(x+x_{1})+f(y+y_{1})+c=0$.
Chord of contact from $(x_{1},y_{1})$ outside: $T=0$ with same replacement.

notes.heading: Parabola $y^{2}=4ax$ (right opening) — memorize one, derive the rest
points: Vertex at origin, focus $(a,0)$, directrix $x=-a$, axis $y=0$.
$\text{Latus rectum}$ (focal chord ⊥ axis): length $=4a$, endpoints $(a,\pm 2a)$.
$\text{Parametric point}$: $(at^{2},\ 2at)$; tangent there: $ty = x + at^{2}$; normal: $y = -tx + 2at + at^{3}$.
$\text{Focal chord}$: if $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ are endpoints, $t_{1}t_{2} = -1$.
Other orientations just swap $x$ and $y$ signs: $y^{2}=-4ax$ (opens left), $x^{2}=4ay$ (opens up), $x^{2}=-4ay$ (opens down).

notes.heading: Ellipse $x^{2}/a^{2}+y^{2}/b^{2}=1$ with $a>b$
points: Centre origin, major axis along $x$ ($2a$), minor along $y$ ($2b$).
Eccentricity $e=\sqrt{1-\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}}$; foci $(\pm ae,0)$; directrices $x=\pm a/e$.
$\text{Latus rectum}$ $=\frac{2b^{2}}{a}$; sum of distances from any point to the two foci $=2a$.
$\text{Auxiliary circle}$: $x^{2}+y^{2}=a^{2}$; eccentric angle $\theta$ gives point $(a\cos\theta,\ b\sin\theta)$.
If $b>a$ the major axis is vertical — $\text{swap }a$ and $b$ in all formulas.

notes.heading: Hyperbola $x^{2}/a^{2}-y^{2}/b^{2}=1$
points: Transverse axis $2a$ (along $x$), conjugate $2b$ (along $y$); centre origin.
Eccentricity $e=\sqrt{1+\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}}>1$; foci $(\pm ae,0)$; directrices $x=\pm a/e$.
$\text{Latus rectum}$ $=\frac{2b^{2}}{a}$; difference of distances to foci $=2a$ (absolute).
$\text{Asymptotes}$ $y=\pm\frac{b}{a}x$ — the hyperbola approaches them as $|x|\to\infty$.
$\text{Rectangular hyperbola}$: $xy=c^{2}$ with $e=\sqrt{2}$; parametric $(ct,\ c/t)$.

notes.heading: Common tangent and chord tool ($T=0$, $S_{1}$)
points: For any conic $S=0$, $T=0$ is the $\text{tangent}$ at $(x_{1},y_{1})$ on the curve (replace $x^{2}\to xx_{1}$, $y^{2}\to yy_{1}$, $xy\to (xy_{1}+x_{1}y)/2$, $x\to (x+x_{1})/2$, $y\to (y+y_{1})/2$).
$S_{1}=S(x_{1},y_{1})$ tells $\text{position}$: $S_{1}<0$ inside (for circle/ellipse with positive leading coefficients), $>0$ outside.
Chord with $\text{midpoint}$ $(x_{1},y_{1})$: $T=S_{1}$.
Pair of tangents from $(x_{1},y_{1})$: $SS_{1}=T^{2}$.

traps: For $\text{ellipse}$ check which of $a,b$ is larger — the $\text{major axis}$ is the larger; $e$ formula swaps if $b>a$.
Parabola $y^2=4ax$: $\text{focus}$ is at distance $a$ from vertex along axis; $\text{directrix}$ is $a$ on the $\text{opposite side}$.
When using $T=0$, replace $x$ by $(x+x_1)/2$ and $y$ by $(y+y_1)/2$ for the linear terms — not $xx_1$.
$S_1$ sign for $\text{hyperbola}$ is not the same inside/outside as circle — draw and test.
$\text{Latus rectum}$ for ellipse and hyperbola both equal $2b^2/a$ only when written as $x^2/a^2 \pm y^2/b^2 =1$ with $a$ as transverse/major.

modules.title: Intro to Three Dimensional Geometry

notes.heading: Coordinate system in space
points: Three mutually perpendicular axes $x,y,z$ meet at $O$; the three coordinate planes are $xy$, $yz$, $zx$.
A point $P(x,y,z)$ has $\text{signed distances}$ from the three planes; signs decide the $\text{octant}$ (±,±,±) → $8$ octants.
Distance from $O$ to $P$: $OP=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}$.
Projection of $P$ on $xy$-plane is $(x,y,0)$; on $x$-axis is $(x,0,0)$.

notes.heading: Distance and section formulas
points: Three points are $\text{collinear}$ if the sum of two distances equals the third.
$\text{Section formula}$ (internal, ratio $m:n$): $\left(\frac{mx_{2}+nx_{1}}{m+n},\frac{my_{2}+ny_{1}}{m+n},\frac{mz_{2}+nz_{1}}{m+n}\right)$.
$\text{External}$ division: $\left(\frac{mx_{2}-nx_{1}}{m-n},\cdots\right)$.

$\text{Midpoint}$ is $\left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2},\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2},\frac{z_{1}+z_{2}}{2}\right)$; centroid of $\triangle ABC$ is the average of vertices; centroid of tetrahedron is average of four vertices.

notes.heading: Direction cosines preview (links to Class 12)
points: Direction cosines of a line: $l=\cos\alpha,\ m=\cos\beta,\ n=\cos\gamma$ where $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are angles with positive axes.
$\text{Direction ratios}$ are any numbers $a,b,c$ proportional to $l,m,n$; then $l=\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}$ etc.
Class 12 3D Geometry builds directly on this — $\text{remember the octant signs and the section formula}$.

traps: Signs decide the $\text{octant}$ — $(-1,2,-3)$ and $(1,2,3)$ are $\text{different octants}$.
Section formula: $\text{internal}$ uses $+$; $\text{external}$ uses $-$ — swapping gives the wrong point on the wrong side.
Distance between $P$ and $Q$ is $\text{always non-negative}$; squaring before comparing can hide a mistake — check $\text{collinearity}$ via sum of two distances $=$ third.
Centroid of a tetrahedron is $\text{average of four}$ vertices, not three.

notes.heading: What a limit really means
points: $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ can be made $\text{arbitrarily close}$ to $L$ by taking $x$ $\text{sufficiently close}$ to $a$ (but $x\ne a$).
The $\text{two-sided}$ limit exists iff $\text{left-hand}$ and $\text{right-hand}$ limits both exist and are $\text{equal}$.
If $f(x)$ grows without bound near $a$, we say the limit $\text{does not exist}$ (or is $\pm\infty$).
'Approach' is not 'equal' — the function may be $\text{undefined}$ at $a$ yet have a perfectly good limit there.

notes.heading: Algebra and squeeze
points: $\lim (f\pm g)=\lim f \pm \lim g$, $\lim (fg)=\lim f\cdot\lim g$, $\lim (f/g)=\lim f/\lim g$ provided limits exist and denominator $\ne0$.
$\text{Squeeze}$: if $g(x)\le f(x)\le h(x)$ near $a$ and $\lim g=\lim h=L$, then $\lim f=L$.
Standard squeeze result: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$ ($x$ in $\text{radians}$).
Other standards derived: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^{2}}=\frac12$, $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x}{x}=1$, $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{x}-1}{x}=1$.

notes.heading: Techniques for 0/0 and ∞/∞
points: Try $\text{direct substitution}$ first; if you get a finite number, you are done.
$0/0$: $\text{factorise}$ and $\text{cancel}$ $(x-a)$, or $\text{rationalise}$ (multiply by conjugate) for roots.
$\infty/\infty$: $\text{divide}$ numerator and denominator by the $\text{highest power}$ of $x$.
For $x\to0$ trigonometric forms, use $\frac{\sin x}{x}$ and $\frac{1-\cos x}{x^{2}}$ identities after rearrangement.

notes.heading: Derivative from first principle
points: Definition: $f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ whenever the limit exists.
Using this, $\frac{d}{dx}x^{n}=nx^{n-1}$ (for integer $n$; extended later), $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x$, $\frac{d}{dx}\cos x=-\sin x$.
The $\text{existence}$ of the derivative at $a$ needs the $\text{left and right}$ difference quotients to agree.
Class 12 will extend this with $\text{product, quotient and chain rules}$.

formulas.e: g\le f\le h,\ \lim g=\lim h=L \Rightarrow \lim f=L

traps: $\lim_{x\to0}\sin x / x =1$ only for $x$ in $\text{radians}$ — in $\text{degrees}$ the limit is $\pi/180$.
Cancelling $(x-a)$ is valid only for the $\text{limit}$ ($x\ne a$); you cannot do it in the $\text{function value}$ at $a$.
For $|x|$ or piecewise functions, $\text{check both sides}$ — left and right limits can differ.
$\infty/\infty$ via highest power: $\text{dominant term}$ decides — lower powers vanish.
Derivative from first principle needs $\text{limit }h\to0$ of the $\text{difference quotient}$ — don't differentiate term-by-term in that derivation.

notes.heading: Measures of central tendency
points: $\text{Mean}$: $\bar x = \frac{\sum x_{i}}{n}$ (raw); $\bar x = \frac{\sum f_{i}x_{i}}{\sum f_{i}}$ (grouped).
$\text{Median}$: middle value after sorting; for even $n$ average the two middle values.
$\text{Mode}$: most frequent value; a dataset can have multiple modes.
For $\text{grouped continuous}$ data, class mark $x_{i}=\frac{\text{lower}+\text{upper}}{2}$ represents the class.

notes.heading: Mean deviation
points: Mean deviation about mean: $\frac{1}{n}\sum|x_{i}-\bar x|$; about median: $\frac{1}{n}\sum|x_{i}-\text{median}|$.
For grouped data: $\frac{1}{N}\sum f_{i}|x_{i}-\bar x|$ where $N=\sum f_{i}$.
Mean deviation is $\text{least}$ when taken about the $\text{median}$ (not the mean).

notes.heading: Variance and standard deviation — the JEE core
points: Variance: $\sigma^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum (x_{i}-\bar x)^{2}$; SD: $\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^{2}}$.
$\text{Shortcut}$ (most useful): $\sigma^{2}=\frac{\sum x_{i}^{2}}{n} - \bar x^{2} = \frac{\sum x_{i}^{2}}{n} - \left(\frac{\sum x_{i}}{n}\right)^{2}$.
For grouped data: $\sigma^{2}=\frac{1}{N}\sum f_{i}(x_{i}-\bar x)^{2}$ and similarly $\sigma^{2}=\frac{\sum f_{i}x_{i}^{2}}{N} - \bar x^{2}$.
$\text{Step deviation}$: let $d_{i}=\frac{x_{i}-A}{h}$ then $\bar x=A+h\bar d$ and $\sigma_{x}=h\sigma_{d}$ (variance scales with $h^{2}$).
Combined mean of two groups: $\bar x = \frac{n_{1}\bar x_{1}+n_{2}\bar x_{2}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}$.

notes.heading: Coefficient of variation
points: $CV = \frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100\%$ — $\text{unit-free}$; smaller $CV$ means more $\text{consistent}$ data.
Use $CV$ to compare variability of datasets with $\text{different means}$.
Outliers increase $\sigma$ sharply; median-based measures are more $\text{robust}$.

traps: In grouped data, $x_i$ is the $\text{class mark}$, not the lower limit.
Variance shortcut needs $\sum x_i^2 / n$ $\text{minus}$ $\bar x^2$ — don't forget to $\text{square the mean}$.
For $\text{combined variance}$, you need the combined mean first; don't average the two variances.
$CV$ uses $\bar x$ in denominator — if $\bar x$ is near zero, $CV$ becomes $\text{unstable}$ (avoid).
Mean deviation about $\text{median}$ is $\text{minimal}$ — so if a question asks for least MD, answer is median.

mindmap.subtitle: Class 11 · NCERT Ch 14 — random experiment, events

branches.title: Experiment & sample space
items: Random experiment: outcome not known in advance
Sample space S = all possible outcomes

branches.title: Addition & complement
items: At least one, none, exactly one

notes.heading: Sample space and events
points: A $\text{random experiment}$ is one whose outcome cannot be predicted beforehand; the set of all outcomes is the $\text{sample space}$ $S$.
An $\text{event}$ is a $\text{subset}$ of $S$; e.g. 'getting an even number on a die' $=\{2,4,6\}$.
$\text{Null}$ event $\emptyset$ and $\text{sure}$ event $S$ are extremes.
Events $A$ and $B$ are $\text{mutually exclusive}$ if $A\cap B=\emptyset$; they are $\text{exhaustive}$ if $A\cup B=S$ (or union of many equals $S$).
The $\text{complement}$ $A'$ means '$A$ does not occur'; $A\cup A'=S$ and $A\cap A'=\emptyset$.

notes.heading: Classical probability
points: When all outcomes in $S$ are $\text{equally likely}$, $P(A)=\frac{n(A)}{n(S)}$ where $n(A)$ is the count of favourable outcomes.
Axioms: $0\le P(A)\le1$, $P(S)=1$, $P(\emptyset)=0$.
$P(A')=1-P(A)$ — $\text{the most used shortcut}$: 'at least one' or 'none' often via complement.
Odds in favour $a:b$ means $P=\frac{a}{a+b}$; odds against $a:b$ means $P=\frac{b}{a+b}$.

notes.heading: Addition rule
points: General: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$.
If $A,B$ are $\text{mutually exclusive}$ then $P(A\cap B)=0$ and $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$.
For three events: $P(A\cup B\cup C)=\sum P -\sum P(\text{pairwise intersections}) + P(A\cap B\cap C)$.
'At least one of $A,B$' $=P(A\cup B)$; 'none' $=1-P(A\cup B)$; 'exactly one' $=P(A)+P(B)-2P(A\cap B)$.

notes.heading: Counting for probability (link to P&C)
points: '$n(A)$' is almost always a $\text{P&C count}$: arrange, choose, or count numbers — so recap $P(n,r)$ and $C(n,r)$.
For $\text{cards}$: $52$ total, $4$ suits $\times13$ ranks, $26$ red/$26$ black, $12$ face cards, $4$ aces.
For $\text{dice}$: $n(S)=6^{k}$ for $k$ dice; for $\text{coins}$: $2^{k}$.
For $\text{balls}$ drawn with/without replacement, decide whether order matters (usually not, so use combinations).

notes.heading: JEE traps in Class 11 probability
points: 'Equally likely' must hold before using $n(A)/n(S)$; for a $\text{biased}$ coin or die you need given probabilities.
'At least one' via complement: $1-P(\text{none})$ is almost always shorter than direct summing.
'$A$ or $B$' means $A\cup B$, not $A\cap B$.
For overlapping events, $\text{subtract the intersection once}$ — otherwise you double count.

formulas.e: P(A\cup B\cup C)=\sum P -\sum P(A\cap B)+P(A\cap B\cap C)

traps: Don't use $n(A)/n(S)$ if outcomes are $\text{not equally likely}$ (biased).
'At least one' via complement is $1-P(\text{none})$, but $\text{none}$ must be computed correctly via complement of union.
'$A$ and $B$' ($A\cap B$) vs '$A$ or $B$' ($A\cup B$) — mixing them loses marks.
When counting $n(A)$, $\text{double-counting}$ overlapping cases is common — use inclusion–exclusion.

modules.title: Relations & Functions — Class 12

mindmap.subtitle: Class 12 · NCERT Ch 1 — types of relations & functions

branches.title: Composition & invertibility
items: Inverse graph is mirror in y=x

notes.heading: Relations — test each property
points: $\text{Reflexive}$: $(a,a)\in R$ for every $a$ in the set.
$\text{Symmetric}$: $(a,b)\in R \Rightarrow (b,a)\in R$.
$\text{Transitive}$: $(a,b),(b,c)\in R \Rightarrow (a,c)\in R$.
$\text{Equivalence}$ = reflexive + symmetric + transitive; it $\text{partitions}$ the set into disjoint equivalence classes.
Example: 'congruent mod $n$' is an equivalence relation on $Z$.

notes.heading: Functions — shape words that get tested
points: $\text{One-one}$ (injective): $f(a)=f(b) \Rightarrow a=b$; a horizontal line cuts the graph $\text{at most once}$.
$\text{Onto}$ (surjective): every element of the $\text{co-domain}$ has a pre-image; check $\text{range}=\text{co-domain}$.
$\text{Bijective}$: both one-one and onto — exactly one inverse exists.
$\text{Many-one}$: two distinct domain elements share the same image; $\text{into}$: range is a $\text{proper subset}$ of co-domain.
Important: $\text{onto vs into}$ depends on the declared co-domain, not just the values you happen to get.

notes.heading: Composition and inverse
points: $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$ exists only when $\text{range}(f)\subseteq\text{Dom}(g)$.
Composition is $\text{associative}$ but $\text{not commutative}$ in general.
$f$ is $\text{invertible}$ iff it is $\text{bijective}$; then $f^{-1}(y)=x \iff f(x)=y$.
Graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $\text{mirror images}$ in the line $y=x$.
$(f\circ g)^{-1}=g^{-1}\circ f^{-1}$ (socks-and-shoes rule).

notes.heading: Binary operations
points: A binary operation $*$ on $A$ is a function $*:A\times A\to A$.
$*$ is $\text{commutative}$ if $a*b=b*a$ for all $a,b$; $\text{associative}$ if $(a*b)*c=a*(b*c)$.
$e$ is $\text{identity}$ if $a*e=e*a=a$ for all $a$.
$b$ is the $\text{inverse}$ of $a$ if $a*b=b*a=e$.
Check all properties by $\text{testing with general elements}$, not just examples.

notes.heading: Counts that JEE loves
points: Number of $\text{relations}$ from $A$ to $B$ ($|A|=m, |B|=n$): $2^{mn}$.
Number of $\text{functions}$ $A\to B$: $n^{m}$; number of $\text{one-one}$ functions (if $n\ge m$): $P(n,m)=\frac{n!}{(n-m)!}$; if $n<m$ it is $0$.
Number of $\text{onto}$ functions $A\to B$ with $|A|=m, |B|=n$: $n^{m} - C(n,1)(n-1)^{m}+C(n,2)(n-2)^{m}-\cdots$ (inclusion–exclusion).
Number of $\text{reflexive}$ relations on $n$ elements: $2^{n^{2}-n}$; $\text{symmetric}$: $2^{n(n+1)/2}$.

formulas.d: All diagonal pairs must be in relation.
g after f; domain check needed.

traps: 'Number of relations' vs 'number of functions' — $\text{relations}$ count subsets of $A\times B$, $\text{functions}$ count assignments with exactly one image each.
Reflexive needs $(a,a)$ for $\text{every}$ $a$ — missing even one $\text{breaks}$ it.
Checking $\text{onto}$ requires the $\text{declared co-domain}$; changing the co-domain can change onto to into.
$(g\circ f)$ exists only if $\text{range}(f)$ fits inside $\text{Dom}(g)$ — domain check is a $\text{favourite trap}$.
$f^{-1}$ exists iff $f$ is $\text{bijective}$; merely one-one is not enough if not onto the stated co-domain.

modules.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions

notes.heading: Principal values — remember the ranges
points: $\sin^{-1}x$: $x\in[-1,1]$, $y\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ — $\text{odd}$, increasing through origin.
$\tan^{-1}x$: $x\in R$, $y\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ — $\text{odd}$; $\cot^{-1}x$: $y\in(0,\pi)$.
$\sec^{-1}x$: $|x|\ge1$, $y\in[0,\pi]\setminus\{\pi/2\}$; $\text{cosec}^{-1}x$: similar with $y\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]\setminus\{0\}$.
Principal value is the $\text{unique}$ value of the inverse in its defined interval — $\text{always answer inside it}$.

notes.heading: Basic identities
points: $\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ for $x\in R$.
$\sec^{-1}x+\text{cosec}^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ for $|x|\ge1$.

notes.heading: Sum and difference of tan⁻¹ — the big chapter
points: $\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+y}{1-xy}\right)$ if $xy<1$; if $xy>1$ you must add $\pm\pi$ to bring the result into $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$.
$\tan^{-1}x-\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x-y}{1+xy}\right)$ (always in principal range when the RHS is between $-\pi/2$ and $\pi/2$).
Alternative double: $2\tan^{-1}x=\sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{1+x^{2}}=\cos^{-1}\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}$.
Best strategy: $\text{convert everything to tan}^{-1}$ before adding, then handle the $\pi$ correction if needed.

notes.heading: Conversions — make the sum possible
points: $\sin^{-1}x=\cos^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$ for $0\le x\le1$ (sign matters for negative $x$).
When you see $\sin^{-1}x+\sin^{-1}y$, convert both to $\tan^{-1}$: $\sin^{-1}x=\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$.

notes.heading: Solving equations
points: For $\sin^{-1}x=\theta$, immediately write $x=\sin\theta$ and check domain.
Use $\text{graphical}$ insight: $\sin^{-1}$ is increasing, so $\sin^{-1}a < \sin^{-1}b \iff a<b$.
If an equation mixes $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$, use $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\pi/2$ to reduce to one type.
Always $\text{verify}$ the final $x$ satisfies the original domains and principal ranges.

traps: Principal value must lie in the $\text{defined interval}$ — $\sin^{-1}(1/2)=30°$ not $150°$.
$\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y$ needs the $\pm\pi$ correction when $xy>1$ — $\text{skipping it}$ gives a value outside $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$.
$\sin^{-1}x$ requires $|x|\le1$ — any $x$ outside has $\text{no real inverse}$.
When converting $\sin^{-1}x$ to $\tan^{-1}$, check the $\text{sign}$ for negative $x$; $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ is $\text{positive}$ always.
Equations: $\text{verify}$ the solution satisfies the original equation — extraneous roots appear after $\tan$ conversion.

modules.title: Matrices

branches.title: Types & order
items: Row, column, square, diagonal, scalar, unit I
Equal matrices: same order, same elements

branches.title: Operations
items: Multiplication AB: columns of A = rows of B

notes.heading: Basics and types
points: Order $m\times n$ means $m$ rows, $n$ columns; $a_{ij}$ is the element in row $i$, column $j$.
$\text{Square}$ matrix: $m=n$; $\text{diagonal}$: non-zero only on the principal diagonal; $\text{scalar}$: diagonal all equal $k$; $\text{unit/identity}$ $I_{n}$: scalar with $k=1$.
$\text{Symmetric}$: $A^{T}=A$ ($a_{ij}=a_{ji}$); $\text{skew-symmetric}$: $A^{T}=-A$ ($a_{ij}=-a_{ji}$, diagonal $=0$).
Every $\text{square}$ matrix can be written uniquely as $\frac12(A+A^{T}) + \frac12(A-A^{T})$ (symmetric + skew-symmetric).

notes.heading: Addition, scalar, transpose
points: $A+B$ exists only for $\text{same order}$; performed $\text{element-wise}$.
$kA$: multiply $\text{every element}$ by $k$.
$(AB)^{T}=B^{T}A^{T}$ — $\text{reverse order}$.

notes.heading: Multiplication — the heavy part
points: $AB$ exists only if $\text{columns of }A = \text{rows of }B$; if $A$ is $m\times n$ and $B$ is $n\times p$, then $AB$ is $m\times p$.
Entry $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k} A_{ik}B_{kj}$ (row $i$ dot column $j$).
$AB \ne BA$ in general; even when both exist, $AB=0$ does $\text{not imply}$ $A=0$ or $B=0$.
$AI = IA = A$ for identity of appropriate size; $A\cdot0=0$.
Matrix multiplication is $\text{associative}$: $(AB)C=A(BC)$, and $\text{distributive}$: $A(B+C)=AB+AC$.

notes.heading: Invertibility preview (uses determinant)
points: A $\text{square}$ matrix $A$ is invertible (has $A^{-1}$) iff $|A|\ne0$ (non-singular).
If $A^{-1}$ exists, $AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I$ and it is $\text{unique}$.
$A\cdot\text{adj}A = |A|I$ (proved via determinants).
$\text{Elementary operations}$ on rows (or columns) can reduce a matrix to $I$ to find its inverse — the same operations on $I$ give $A^{-1}$.

notes.heading: Time savers
points: For $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$ the $\text{adjoint}$ is $\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a\end{pmatrix}$ — $\text{swap diagonal, negate off-diagonal}$.
If $A$ is $\text{symmetric}$, any power $A^{n}$ is symmetric; if skew, $A^{2}$ is symmetric.
Trace $\text{tr}A = \sum a_{ii}$ satisfies $\text{tr}(AB)=\text{tr}(BA)$.

formulas.d: Columns of A = rows of B.

traps: $A+B$ and $AB$ need $\text{compatible orders}$ — adding $2\times3$ to $3\times2$ is $\text{impossible}$.
$AB=0$ does $\text{not imply}$ $A=0$ or $B=0$ — zero divisors exist for matrices.
$(AB)^T = B^TA^T$, not $A^TB^T$ — $\text{order reverses}$.
For $\text{symmetric + skew}$ decomposition, the two parts are $\frac12(A\pm A^T)$ — don't forget the $1/2$.
Inverse exists only for $\text{square}$ matrices with $\det\ne0$; non-square never has a two-sided inverse.

modules.title: Determinants

branches.title: Properties (row/col ops)
items: Common factor from a row can be taken out
Adding multiple of a row to another → no change

branches.title: JEE properties
items: Determinant of triangular = product of diagonal

notes.heading: Evaluation
points: $\text{2×2}$: $\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc$.

$\text{3×3}$: expand along any row/column using $\text{cofactor expansion}$: $|A|=\sum_{j} a_{ij}C_{ij}$ where $C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$ and $M_{ij}$ is the $2×2$ minor left after deleting row $i$, column $j$.
Sarrus' rule for $3×3$ works but $\text{cofactor}$ is safer when properties are used.
$\text{Triangular}$ matrix (upper or lower) has determinant = $\text{product of diagonal}$ entries.

notes.heading: Key properties (use before expanding)
points: Swapping two rows (or columns) $\text{changes sign}$.
If a row (or column) is multiplied by $k$, the determinant is $\text{multiplied}$ by $k$; taking $k$ common from $\text{each}$ of $n$ rows multiplies by $k^{n}$.
If two rows (or columns) are $\text{identical}$ or $\text{proportional}$, $|A|=0$.
Adding a multiple of one row to another $\text{does not change}$ the determinant ($R_{i}\to R_{i}+kR_{j}$).
$|kA| = k^{n}|A|$ for $n\times n$ matrix $A$.

notes.heading: Adjoint and inverse
points: $\text{Cofactor matrix}$ $C=[C_{ij}]$; $\text{adj}A = C^{T}$.
Fundamental: $A\cdot\text{adj}A = \text{adj}A\cdot A = |A|I$.
If $|A|\ne0$, $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}A$; if $|A|=0$, $A$ is $\text{singular}$ (no inverse).
For $2×2$, $\text{adj}\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a\end{pmatrix}$.

notes.heading: Geometry and linear systems
points: Area of $\triangle$ with vertices $(x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2}),(x_{3},y_{3})$: $\Delta = \frac12\left|\begin{matrix} x_{1}&y_{1}&1\\x_{2}&y_{2}&1\\x_{3}&y_{3}&1\end{matrix}\right|$.
Collinearity $\iff \Delta=0$.

For system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ with $A$ $3×3$: if $|A|\ne0$, $\text{unique solution}$ $\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$; Cramer's rule $x_{i}=\frac{|A_{i}|}{|A|}$ where $A_{i}$ is $A$ with column $i$ replaced by $\mathbf{b}$.
If $|A|=0$ and $(\text{adj}A)\mathbf{b}\ne0$ the system is $\text{inconsistent}$ (no solution); if $(\text{adj}A)\mathbf{b}=0$ it may have $\text{infinitely many}$ solutions.

notes.heading: JEE shortcuts
points: Apply $\text{row operations}$ to create $\text{zeros}$ before expanding — it saves time and reduces errors.
If a row is a $\text{linear combination}$ of other rows, determinant $=0$ without expanding.
For $\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ b & c & a \\ c & a & b\end{vmatrix}$ style cyclic determinants, try $C_{1}\to C_{1}+C_{2}+C_{3}$.

traps: Taking $k$ common from $\text{each}$ of $n$ rows multiplies det by $k^n$, not $k$.
Using $R_i\to kR_i$ $\text{scales}$ the determinant — don't do it before $\text{comparison}$ without dividing back.
For area of triangle, don't forget the $1/2$ and the $\text{absolute value}$.
$A^{-1}=\text{adj}A/|A|$ needs $|A|\ne0$ — $\text{check}$ before applying Cramer's rule.
$|AB|=|A||B|$ but $A+B$ has no such simple rule — $\text{don't split}$ $|A+B|$.

modules.title: Continuity & Differentiability

branches.title: Continuity
items: f continuous at a if lim f = f(a)
Types of discontinuity: removable, jump, infinite
Algebra: sum/product/quotient of continuous is continuous

branches.title: Differentiability
items: f′ exists if left & right derivatives match

branches.title: Standard derivatives
items: Power, sin, cos, tan, sec, cot, cosec

notes.heading: Continuity at a point
points: $f$ is $\text{continuous}$ at $a$ if $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)$; this needs $f(a)$ defined, the limit exists, and they are $\text{equal}$.
Discontinuities: $\text{removable}$ (limit exists but $\ne f(a)$), $\text{jump}$ (left $\ne$ right), $\text{infinite}$ (blows up).
$\text{Algebra}$: sum, difference, product of continuous functions is continuous; quotient is continuous where denominator $\ne0$; composition of continuous is continuous.
Standard continuous functions: polynomials, $\sin$, $\cos$, $e^{x}$ everywhere; $\tan$ away from $\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi$; $\ln x$ for $x>0$.
$\text{Intermediate Value}$: if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $k$ is between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then $f(c)=k$ for some $c\in(a,b)$.

notes.heading: Differentiability — stronger than continuity
points: $f$ is $\text{differentiable}$ at $a$ if $\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$ exists (left and right limits $\text{match}$).
$\text{Differentiability} \Rightarrow \text{continuity}$; converse is $\text{false}$ (e.g. $|x|$ is continuous at $0$ but not differentiable there).
$\text{Corner}$ (like $|x|$ at $0$), $\text{cusp}$, or $\text{vertical tangent}$ ($\frac1{x}$) make differentiability fail.
To test piecewise functions, compute $\text{LHD}=\lim_{h\to0^{-}}$ and $\text{RHD}=\lim_{h\to0^{+}}$ — differentiability needs $LHD=RHD$.

notes.heading: Differentiation toolbox
points: $\text{Power}$: $\frac{d}{dx}x^{n}=nx^{n-1}$.
$\text{Product}$: $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$; $\text{Quotient}$: $\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)'=\frac{u'v-uv'}{v^{2}}$.
$\text{Chain}$: if $y=f(u)$, $u=g(x)$ then $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}$; in practice write $\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)$.
$\text{Implicit}$: differentiate both sides, treat $y$ as function of $x$, collect $dy/dx$.
$\text{Logarithmic}$: for $y=\frac{u^{a}v^{b}}{w^{c}}$ take $\ln$, then differentiate; essential for $y=x^{x}$.

notes.heading: Standard derivatives to memorize
points: $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x$, $\frac{d}{dx}\cos x=-\sin x$, $\frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^{2}x$, $\frac{d}{dx}\cot x=-\text{cosec}^{2}x$, $\frac{d}{dx}\sec x=\sec x\tan x$, $\frac{d}{dx}\text{cosec }x=-\text{cosec }x\cot x$.
$\frac{d}{dx}e^{x}=e^{x}$, $\frac{d}{dx}a^{x}=a^{x}\ln a$, $\frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac1x$, $\frac{d}{dx}\log_{a}x=\frac1{x\ln a}$.

$\text{Parametric}$: if $x=\phi(t), y=\psi(t)$ then $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$; $\text{second order}$: $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)$ (treat as function of $x$).

notes.heading: Mean Value Theorems
points: $\text{Rolle's}$: if $f$ continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f(a)=f(b)$, then $f'(c)=0$ for some $c\in(a,b)$.
$\text{Lagrange (LMVT)}$: $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=f'(c)$ for some $c$ — $\text{slope of chord = slope of tangent}$.
Corollary: if $f'(x)=0$ on an interval then $f$ is $\text{constant}$ there; if $f'>0$ on $(a,b)$ then $f$ is $\text{strictly increasing}$ on $[a,b]`.
Use LMVT to $\text{bound}$ functions: e.g. $|\sin x|\le|x|$.

formulas.d: Three conditions: defined, limit exists, equal.

traps: Checking $\text{continuity}$ needs $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)$ ($x\ne a$) — don't substitute $a$ inside a $\text{piecewise}$ definition that changes at $a$.
$|x|$ is $\text{continuous}$ everywhere but $\text{not differentiable}$ at $0$ — never claim 'continuous so diffable'.
For $\text{piecewise differentiability}$, compute $LHD$ and $RHD$ from the $\text{definition}$; using the derivative formula of each piece and substituting $a$ can misfire when pieces meet.
$\ln$ differentiation needs $x>0$; for $\ln|x|$ use $|x|$ correspondingly.
LMVT and Rolle need $\text{continuity on closed}$ $[a,b]$ and $\text{differentiability on open}$ $(a,b)$ — check endpoints.

modules.title: Application of Derivatives

branches.title: Rate of change
items: Related rates: differentiate w.r.t. t, substitute

branches.title: Tangents & normals
items: Slope of tangent = dy/dx at point

branches.title: Maxima & minima
items: Absolute max/min on [a,b]: check endpoints too

notes.heading: Rate, approximation, tangent — one idea
points: $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is the $\text{instantaneous rate}$ of $y$ with respect to $x$; $\frac{dy}{dt}$ is the rate in $\text{time}$.
For $\text{related rates}$, write the geometric relation (e.g. $V=\frac43\pi r^{3}$), then $\text{differentiate}$ w.r.t. $t$ and substitute the instant data.
$\text{Approximation}$: $\Delta y \approx dy = f'(x)\Delta x$; relative error $\frac{\Delta y}{y}\approx\frac{dy}{y}$.
$\text{Tangent}$ at $(x_{1},y_{1})$: $y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1})$ where $m=\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(x_{1},y_{1})}$; $\text{normal}$ slope $m_{n}=-1/m$ (when $m\ne0$).
If the curve is given $\text{implicitly}$ or $\text{parametrically}$, find $dy/dx$ first, then evaluate at the point.

notes.heading: Increasing / decreasing
points: $f'(x)>0$ on an interval ⇒ $f$ $\text{strictly increasing}$ there; $f'(x)<0$ ⇒ $\text{strictly decreasing}$.
Points where $f'(x)=0$ or $f'(x)$ $\text{does not exist}$ are $\text{critical points}$ — monotonicity can change only there.
$\text{First derivative test}$: sign of $f'$ left and right of a critical point decides increase/decrease.
If $f'(x)\ge0$ everywhere and $>0$ somewhere, $f$ is $\text{non-decreasing}$; strictness matters in JEE wording.

notes.heading: Maxima and minima — local vs absolute
points: $\text{Local max}$ at $c$ if $f(c)\ge f(x)$ near $c$; $\text{local min}$ if $\le$.
Candidates: $\text{critical points}$ and points where $f'$ $\text{does not exist}$.
$\text{First derivative test}$: sign of $f'$: $+\to-$ gives max, $-\to+$ gives min.
$\text{Second derivative test}$: if $f'(c)=0$ then $f''(c)>0 \Rightarrow$ local min, $f''(c)<0 \Rightarrow$ local max; if $f''(c)=0$ the test $\text{fails}$ (use first derivative).
$\text{Absolute}$ max/min on $[a,b]$: evaluate $f$ at all critical points $\text{inside}$ $(a,b)$ $\text{and}$ at $a,b$ — the largest is the absolute max.

notes.heading: Applied maxima — the word problems
points: Model: write the quantity to optimise (area, volume, cost) as a $\text{function of one variable}$ using the constraint to eliminate the other variable.
Domain of that variable comes from the $\text{feasibility}$ (lengths $>0$, etc.).
Set $\frac{d}{dx}=0$, test candidates; $\text{verify}$ it is a max (not min) via sign change or second derivative.
Classic: $\text{box with no lid}$, $\text{largest cylinder in cone}$, $\text{fence with fixed length}$ — practice the $\text{constraint elimination}$ step.

formulas.d: m≠0; if m=0 normal is vertical.

traps: For $\text{related rates}$, $\text{differentiate first}$, $\text{substitute values after}$ — substituting too early loses the derivative term.
At a $\text{cusp}$ or $\text{corner}$ $f'$ does not exist; such points are $\text{critical}$ even though $f'=0$ does not hold there.
Second derivative test $\text{fails}$ when $f''(c)=0$ — switch to $\text{first derivative}$ sign change.
For $\text{absolute}$ max/min on a $\text{closed interval}$, always check the $\text{endpoints}$; the extremum may be at the boundary even if interior critical points exist.
In $\text{optimisation word problems}$, the $\text{domain}$ of the single-variable function must respect $\text{feasibility}$ (e.g. radius $>0$) — discard extraneous critical points outside.

modules.title: Integrals

notes.heading: Indefinite — family of antiderivatives
points: $\int f(x)dx = F(x)+C$ where $F'(x)=f(x)$; the $+C$ is $\text{mandatory}$ for indefinite integrals.
$\int x^{n}dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$ ($n\ne-1$); $\int \frac{dx}{x}=\ln|x|+C$.
$\int e^{x}dx=e^{x}+C$, $\int a^{x}dx=\frac{a^{x}}{\ln a}+C$.
$\int \sin x\,dx=-\cos x+C$, $\int \cos x\,dx=\sin x+C$, $\int \sec^{2}x\,dx=\tan x+C$, $\int \text{cosec}^{2}x\,dx=-\cot x+C$, $\int \sec x\tan x\,dx=\sec x+C$.
$\int \frac{dx}{1+x^{2}}=\tan^{-1}x+C$, $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}=\sin^{-1}x+C$.

notes.heading: Substitution
points: If the integrand contains $f(g(x))\cdot g'(x)$, set $t=g(x)$.
$\text{Trigonometric}$: for $\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$ put $x=a\sin\theta$; for $\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}$ put $x=a\tan\theta$; for $\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}$ put $x=a\sec\theta$.
For $\int \frac{dx}{a\sin x+b\cos x}$ use $t=\tan\frac{x}{2}$ (Weierstrass) or divide numerator/denominator by $\cos x$.
Always $\text{change limits}$ when substituting in a definite integral; for indefinite, convert back to $x$.

notes.heading: Partial fractions and by parts
points: $\text{Proper}$ fraction (degree numerator < denominator): factor denominator and split; $\text{improper}$: do $\text{polynomial division}$ first.
Forms: $\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x-b}$, $\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{(x-a)^{2}}$, $\frac{Ax+B}{x^{2}+a^{2}}$.
$\text{By parts}$: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$; choose $u$ by $\text{ILATE}$ ($I$–inverse, $L$–log, $A$–algebraic, $T$–trig, $E$–exponential).
Repeated by parts or tabular method for $\int x^{n}e^{x}$; $\int e^{x}(f+f')dx = e^{x}f(x)+C$.

notes.heading: Standard forms to memorize
points: $\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{a}+C$, $\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}-a^{2}}=\frac1{2a}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right|+C$.
$\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}}=\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}\right|+C$, $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}=\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a}+C$.
$\int \sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}dx = \frac{x}{2}\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}+\frac{a^{2}}{2}\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}\right|+C$.

notes.heading: Definite properties — score without computing
points: $\int_{a}^{b} f(x)dx = F(b)-F(a)$ (FTC).
Reversal: $\int_{a}^{b} f = -\int_{b}^{a} f$; splitting: $\int_{a}^{b}=\int_{a}^{c}+\int_{c}^{b}$.
$\int_{a}^{b} f(x)dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(a+b-x)dx$ ($\text{King property}$) — $\text{the most used JEE trick}$.
$\int_{0}^{a} f(x)dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a-x)dx$ (special case).
$\text{Even/odd}$: if $f(-x)=-f(x)$ (odd) then $\int_{-a}^{a} f=0$; if $f(-x)=f(x)$ (even) then $\int_{-a}^{a} f=2\int_{0}^{a} f$.
$\int_{0}^{2a} f(x)dx = \begin{cases} 2\int_{0}^{a} f(x)dx & f(2a-x)=f(x) \\ 0 & f(2a-x)=-f(x)\end{cases}$.

traps: For $\text{indefinite}$ integrals, $+C$ is $\text{mandatory}$ — missing it is marked wrong.
Substitution in $\text{definite}$ integrals needs $\text{new limits}$; keeping old limits with new variable gives wrong sign.
For $\int_{-a}^{a} f$, first test $f(-x)$ — blindly computing without $\text{even/odd}$ wastes time.
$\text{ILATE}$ order chooses $u$; reversing it makes by-parts $\text{harder}$, not wrong, but longer.
$\int e^x(f+f') = e^x f$ only when the integrand is $\text{exactly}$ $e^x(f+f')$ — missing factor needs $\text{adjustment}$.

modules.title: Application of Integrals — Area

branches.title: JEE patterns
items: Area with modulus splits at kink

notes.heading: Area under a curve
points: If $y=f(x)\ge0$ on $[a,b]$, the area between the curve, $x$-axis, and $x=a,b$ is $A=\int_{a}^{b} f(x)dx$.
If $f(x)\le0$, $\int f$ is negative; the $\text{geometric area}$ is $\left|\int f\right|$.
For area between curve and $y$-axis, integrate w.r.t. $y$: $A=\int_{c}^{d} x\,dy$ where $x=g(y)$.
If the curve crosses the axis, $\text{split}$ the integral at the zero crossing.

notes.heading: Area between two curves
points: If $y_{top}(x) \ge y_{bottom}(x)$ on $[a,b]$, then $A=\int_{a}^{b} [y_{top}-y_{bottom}]dx$.
Limits $a,b$ are the $x$-coordinates of the $\text{intersection points}$ — solve $y_{top}=y_{bottom}$.
Use $\text{symmetry}$: circle and ellipse areas can be done as $4\times$ first-quadrant area.
For $x$ as function of $y$ when curves are more naturally $x=g(y)$, use $A=\int [x_{right}-x_{left}]dy$.

notes.heading: Standard areas with circles & conics
points: Circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=a^{2}$: $A=\pi a^{2}$; in first quadrant $A_{quad}=\frac{\pi a^{2}}{4}=\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}dx$.
Area between $y^{2}=4ax$ and $x=k$ is $\frac{8}{3}a^{1/2}k^{3/2}$? Derive via $\int 2\sqrt{4ax}\,dx$.
For $y=|x|$ type regions, $\text{split}$ at the $\text{kink}$ ($x=0$).

notes.heading: Strategy in exam
points: $\text{Sketch}$ in 10 seconds: intercepts, symmetry, intersection.
Label which curve is $\text{on top}$; test with a point between limits.
If modulus present like $|x|+|y|\le k$, the region is a $\text{rhombus}$ with area $2k^{2}$; verify by sketch.
For $\text{parameter}$ problems, find intersection in terms of parameter, then integrate.

formulas.d: Between y²=4ax and x=k is 2∫ y_top dx.

traps: $\int_a^b f(x)dx$ can be $\text{negative}$ if $f<0$ — geometric area needs $\text{absolute value}$.
Between two curves, $\text{identify top vs bottom}$ correctly; swapping gives $\text{negative area}$.
When the region is described with $x$ as function of $y$, integrating $y_{top}-y_{bottom}$ w.r.t. $x$ is $\text{wrong}$ — switch to $dy$.
For $|x|+|y|$ type, don't integrate blindly — $\text{sketch}$ the diamond; integration $\text{splits}$ into four triangles.
Limits are $\text{intersection points}$ — solving $y_{top}=y_{bottom}$ incorrectly $\text{shifts}$ the entire integral.

modules.title: Differential Equations

branches.title: Order & degree
items: Degree = power of highest derivative (after removing radicals)

branches.title: General & particular solution
items: General contains arbitrary constants (as many as order)

branches.title: Variable separable
items: Rewrite as g(y) dy = f(x) dx → integrate both sides
Include constant C, solve for y

branches.title: Homogeneous & linear
items: IF = e^{∫P dx}, solution y·IF = ∫ Q·IF dx

notes.heading: Order and degree
points: $\text{Order}$ is the order of the highest derivative present; $\text{degree}$ is the power of that derivative after the equation is made $\text{free of radicals and fractions in derivatives}$.
Example: $(y'')^{2}+y'=0$ has order $2$, degree $2$; $\sqrt{y''}+y=0$ becomes $y''=y^{2}$ after squaring, so order $2$, degree $1$.
A $\text{linear}$ differential equation has the dependent variable and its derivatives only to power $1$ and not multiplied together.
The $\text{general solution}$ of an $n$-th order equation contains $n$ $\text{arbitrary constants}$.

notes.heading: Variable separable — the first technique to try
points: Rewrite so that all $y$ terms with $dy$ are on one side and all $x$ terms with $dx$ on the other: $g(y)dy = f(x)dx$.
Integrate: $\int g(y)dy = \int f(x)dx + C$.
If an $\text{initial condition}$ $y(x_{0})=y_{0}$ is given, put it to find $C$ (particular solution).
Do not forget $\pm$ when square roots appear after integration.

notes.heading: Homogeneous equations
points: An equation $M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0$ is $\text{homogeneous}$ if $M,N$ are homogeneous of the same degree, equivalently $dy/dx = f(y/x)$.
Put $y=vx$ ($v$ is function of $x$); then $\frac{dy}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx}$, and the equation becomes $\text{separable}$ in $v,x$.
After solving for $v$, substitute back $v=y/x$.
Test homogeneity quickly: replace $x\to\lambda x,\ y\to\lambda y$ — the factor $\lambda^{k}$ cancels to the same degree.

notes.heading: Linear first-order — the IF method (most asked)
points: Standard form: $\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y = Q(x)$ where $P,Q$ are functions of $x$ alone (or constants).
$\text{Integrating factor}$: $IF = e^{\int P(x)dx}$.
Solution: $y\cdot IF = \int Q(x)\cdot IF\,dx + C$.
If the equation is linear in $x$ (i.e. $\frac{dx}{dy}+P_{1}(y)x = Q_{1}(y)$), then $IF = e^{\int P_{1}(y)dy}$ and $x\cdot IF = \int Q_{1}\cdot IF\,dy + C$.
$\text{Memorize}$: the left side always becomes $\frac{d}{dx}(y\cdot IF)$ after multiplying by $IF$.

notes.heading: Orthogonal trajectories (JEE flavour)
points: Family of curves $F(x,y,c)=0$ has differential equation gotten by $\text{differentiating}$ and eliminating $c$.
Orthogonal family: replace $\frac{dy}{dx}$ by $-\frac{dx}{dy}$ (negative reciprocal slope) and solve the new differential equation.
Example: family $y=cx$ gives $dy/dx=y/x$; orthogonal family satisfies $dy/dx=-x/y$ → $x^{2}+y^{2}=C$.

traps: Degree is defined only after the equation is $\text{free of radicals}$ in derivatives — squaring can change it.
For $\text{linear}$ $dy/dx+Py=Q$, $P$ must be function of $x$ $\text{alone}$; if it contains $y$, swap to $dx/dy$ form.
While computing $IF=e^{\int Pdx}$, don't forget the constant is $\text{absorbed}$ — $IF$ itself needs no $+C$.
In $\text{separable}$, don't divide by an expression that could be $0$ without noting the $\text{lost solution}$ (e.g. $y=0$).
Orthogonal trajectories need $\text{eliminate the constant}$ $c$ $\text{before}$ replacing $dy/dx$ with $-dx/dy$.

modules.title: Vector Algebra

branches.title: Basics & types
items: Position vector, unit vector, zero vector

notes.heading: Vectors — language
points: A $\text{vector}$ has $\text{magnitude}$ and $\text{direction}$; its $\text{magnitude}$ is its length.
$\text{Position vector}$ of $P(x,y,z)$ w.r.t. origin $O$ is $\vec{OP}=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$.
$\text{Unit vector}$ in direction $\vec a$: $\hat a = \frac{\vec a}{|\vec a|}$; $\text{zero vector}$ $\vec0$ has $0$ magnitude, arbitrary direction.
Two vectors are $\text{collinear}$ if they lie on same or parallel lines; $\text{coplanar}$ if they lie in one plane.
$\vec a = \vec b$ means same magnitude and direction; $\vec a = -\vec b$ means opposite.

notes.heading: Addition and section formula
points: $\text{Triangle law}$: $\vec{AB}+\vec{BC}=\vec{AC}$; $\text{parallelogram law}$: diagonal $= \vec a+\vec b$.
Vector addition is $\text{commutative}$ and $\text{associative}$.
$\text{Section formula}$: point dividing $AB$ ($\vec a$, $\vec b$) in ratio $m:n$ has position vector $\frac{m\vec b+n\vec a}{m+n}$ (internal; external uses $-$).
Midpoint is $\frac{\vec a+\vec b}{2}$; centroid of $\triangle ABC$ is $\frac{\vec a+\vec b+\vec c}{3}$.

notes.heading: Dot product — angles and projections
points: $\vec a\cdot\vec b = |\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the $\text{smaller}$ angle ($0\le\theta\le\pi$) between them.
$\vec a\cdot\vec b = 0 \iff \vec a\perp\vec b$ (for non-zero vectors).
$\text{Projection}$ of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$: $\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}$ (scalar), vector projection $\left(\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|^{2}}\right)\vec b$.
Properties: $\vec a\cdot\vec a=|\vec a|^{2}$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec b\cdot\vec a$, and $(k\vec a)\cdot\vec b=k(\vec a\cdot\vec b)$.
$\text{Work done}$ by force $\vec F$ through displacement $\vec d$ is $W=\vec F\cdot\vec d$.

notes.heading: Cross product — area and direction
points: $\vec a\times\vec b = |\vec a||\vec b|\sin\theta\,\hat n$, where $\hat n$ is $\perp$ to both by right-hand rule.
$|\vec a\times\vec b| = $ area of $\text{parallelogram}$ on $\vec a,\vec b$; $\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|=$ area of $\triangle$.
$\vec a\times\vec b = -\vec b\times\vec a$; $\vec a\times\vec a=\vec0$; if $\vec a\parallel\vec b$ then $\vec a\times\vec b=\vec0$.
In components: $\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\a_{1}&a_{2}&a_{3}\\b_{1}&b_{2}&b_{3}\end{vmatrix}$.
$\text{Scalar triple}$ $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=$ volume of parallelepiped; $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0 \iff$ coplanar.

notes.heading: Vector triple product
points: $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c) = \vec b(\vec a\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b)$ — $\text{BAC minus CAB}$ rule.
$[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec a]=[\vec c\ \vec a\ \vec b]$ (cyclic), and swaps change sign.
Use scalar triple $=0$ to $\text{test coplanarity}$ quickly; use $|\vec a\times\vec b|$ for $\text{area}$ without angle.

formulas.e: [\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)
\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec b(\vec a\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b)

traps: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$ implies $\perp$ only if both $\vec a,\vec b\ne\vec0$ — $\vec0$ is $\perp$ to everything trivially.
$|\vec a\times\vec b|=0$ means $\parallel$ (or zero), not $\perp$.
$\vec a\times\vec b$ is $\text{anti-commutative}$: swapping $\text{flips sign}$ — forgetting the minus is common.
Scalar triple $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ is $\text{cyclic}$; non-cyclic swap $\text{changes sign}$.
Area of triangle with position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ is $\frac12|(\vec b-\vec a)\times(\vec c-\vec a)|$ — $\text{shift to origin}$ first.

modules.title: Three Dimensional Geometry

branches.title: Direction cosines & ratios
items: Angles α,β,γ with axes → l=cosα, m=cosβ, n=cosγ
DRs of line joining two points: Δx,Δy,Δz

branches.title: Skew, intersection, distance
items: Skew lines: neither parallel nor intersecting

branches.title: Line & plane
items: Line lies in plane if point satisfies & b·n=0
Intersection of two planes is a line

notes.heading: Direction cosines and ratios
points: If a line makes angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ with the positive $x,y,z$ axes, its $\text{direction cosines}$ are $l=\cos\alpha,\ m=\cos\beta,\ n=\cos\gamma$ and $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$.
$\text{Direction ratios}$ $a,b,c$ are any numbers $\text{proportional}$ to $l,m,n$; then $l=\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}$ (with sign matched).
If $a,b,c$ are DRs, the line's DCs are $\pm a,b,c$ normalized; the $\pm$ gives the two opposite directions.

notes.heading: Straight line
points: $\text{Vector form}$: $\vec r = \vec a + \lambda\vec b$, where $\vec a$ is the position vector of a point on the line and $\vec b$ is the direction vector.
$\text{Cartesian form}$ (symmetric): $\frac{x-x_{1}}{a}=\frac{y-y_{1}}{b}=\frac{z-z_{1}}{c}$ where $(a,b,c)$ are DRs.
$\text{Two-point}$: through $\vec a,\vec b$ direction is $\vec b-\vec a$.
Angle $\theta$ between lines with direction vectors $\vec b_{1},\vec b_{2}$: $\cos\theta=\frac{\vec b_{1}\cdot\vec b_{2}}{|\vec b_{1}||\vec b_{2}|}$; perpendicular iff dot$=0$.
Two lines are $\text{parallel}$ iff $\vec b_{1}\parallel\vec b_{2}$ (DRs proportional); coincident if also sharing a point.

notes.heading: Skew lines and shortest distance
points: $\text{Skew}$ lines are neither parallel nor intersecting — they lie in different planes in space.

For lines $\vec r=\vec a_{1}+\lambda\vec b_{1}$ and $\vec r=\vec a_{2}+\mu\vec b_{2}$, shortest distance $d=\frac{|(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1})\cdot(\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2})|}{|\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}|}$.

If the lines $\text{intersect}$, the numerator $=0$ so $d=0$; for $\text{parallel}$ lines ($\vec b_{1}\parallel\vec b_{2}$), use distance between parallel lines: $d=\frac{|(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1})\times\vec b|}{|\vec b|}$.
Distance from point $\vec a_{0}$ to line $\vec r=\vec a+\lambda\vec b$: $d=\frac{|(\vec a_{0}-\vec a)\times\vec b|}{|\vec b|}$.

notes.heading: Plane
points: $\text{Vector form}$: $(\vec r-\vec a)\cdot\vec n=0$ or $\vec r\cdot\vec n=d$, where $\vec n$ is the $\text{normal}$ to the plane.
$\text{Cartesian form}$: $Ax+By+Cz=D$ with normal $A\hat i+B\hat j+C\hat k$; $\text{intercept form}$: $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}+\frac{z}{c}=1$.
Plane through three non-collinear points: $\left|\begin{matrix} x-x_{1}&y-y_{1}&z-z_{1}\\ x_{2}-x_{1}&y_{2}-y_{1}&z_{2}-z_{1}\\ x_{3}-x_{1}&y_{3}-y_{1}&z_{3}-z_{1}\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
Angle between planes with normals $\vec n_{1},\vec n_{2}$: $\cos\theta=\frac{|\vec n_{1}\cdot\vec n_{2}|}{|\vec n_{1}||\vec n_{2}|}$; planes are $\perp$ iff $\vec n_{1}\cdot\vec n_{2}=0$.

notes.heading: Line and plane interaction
points: Angle $\phi$ between line (direction $\vec b$) and plane (normal $\vec n$): $\sin\phi=\frac{|\vec b\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec b||\vec n|}$ (complement of line-normal angle).
Line lies in plane iff (i) a point of the line satisfies the plane and (ii) $\vec b\cdot\vec n=0$ (line $\perp$ normal).
Line $\parallel$ plane iff $\vec b\cdot\vec n=0$ but point not satisfying plane.
Intersection of two planes $\vec r\cdot\vec n_{1}=d_{1}$ and $\vec r\cdot\vec n_{2}=d_{2}$ is a line with direction $\vec n_{1}\times\vec n_{2}$.

formulas.e: d=\frac{|(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1})\cdot(\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2})|}{|\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}|}

traps: DRs $a,b,c$ are $\text{not}$ DCs until $\text{normalized}$; using $a,b,c$ directly in $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$ is $\text{wrong}$.
For skew $SD$, numerator is $\text{scalar triple}$ $(a_2-a_1)·(b_1×b_2)$ — forgetting the $\text{absolute}$ $\text{above}$ and $\text{magnitude}$ below loses sign and scale.
Line-plane angle uses $\sin$, not $\cos$ — swapping gives complement.
Plane distance needs $\text{constant on one side}$: write as $Ax+By+Cz+D=0$ before applying $|Ax_0+...|/\sqrt{A^2+...}$.
Two lines with $b_1×b_2=0$ are $\text{parallel}$; the skew formula $\text{divides by zero}$ there — use parallel distance instead.

modules.title: Linear Programming

branches.title: Corner point method
items: Find all vertices of feasible region
Max is at a corner (if bounded)
If unbounded, check if Z can go to ±∞

notes.heading: LPP vocabulary
points: $\text{Decision variables}$ $x,y$ are the quantities to choose; they satisfy $x\ge0,\ y\ge0$ in most problems.
$\text{Objective function}$ $Z=ax+by$ is the linear function to $\text{maximize}$ or $\text{minimize}$.
$\text{Constraints}$ are linear inequalities coming from resource limits: $a_{i}x+b_{i}y \le \text{(or }\ge) c_{i}$.
The set of $(x,y)$ satisfying $\text{all}$ constraints is the $\text{feasible region}$; points inside are $\text{feasible solutions}$.
A $\text{feasible region}$ in two variables is always $\text{convex}$ (a polygon, possibly unbounded).

notes.heading: Graphing the feasible region
points: Draw each line $a_{i}x+b_{i}y=c_{i}$ and shade the side given by the inequality ($\text{test (0,0)}$ if line not through origin).
The $\text{intersection}$ of all shaded half-planes is the feasible region — often a polygon with few vertices.
Find $\text{corner points}$ (vertices) by solving pairs of boundary lines simultaneously.
The objective $Z=ax+by=k$ is a $\text{family of parallel lines}$ (iso-profit); sliding $k$ until it just touches the feasible polygon touches a vertex.

notes.heading: Corner point method
points: List all $\text{vertices}$ of the feasible region.
Evaluate $Z$ at each vertex; the $\text{maximum}$ is the vertex with the largest $Z$, the $\text{minimum}$ the smallest.
If the feasible region is $\text{bounded}$, this always gives the optimum.
If $\text{unbounded}$: for 'maximize Z', check if $Z$ can be increased arbitrarily inside the region — if yes, there is $\text{no bounded maximum}$ (unbounded). Similarly for minimize.

notes.heading: Formulation drill (word → math)
points: Read the word problem and $\text{name}$ the variables (e.g. $x$ = units of product A).
Translate each limited resource: 'at most 100 hours' $\to a_{1}x+b_{1}y\le100$.
Write the objective: 'profit is …' $\to Z=\cdots$.
Do not forget $x\ge0,\ y\ge0$ when quantities can't be negative.
Plot, solve, answer in $\text{original words}$ (how many units, max profit).

traps: Forgetting $x\ge0,\ y\ge0$ — the feasible region is $\text{clipped}$ to the first quadrant in most problems.
Choosing the wrong $\text{side}$ for a constraint — always $\text{test (0,0)}$ when possible.

For $\text{unbounded}$ regions, the corner method alone can $\text{mislead}$: an 'unbounded' feasible region may still have a $\text{bounded optimum}$ — check if $ax+by>Z_{max}$ has $\text{no point}$ inside the region.
Optimal solution is always at a $\text{vertex}$ (if it exists) — don't search interior.
If two vertices give the $\text{same optimum}$, the whole $\text{edge}$ between them is optimal.
