notes.heading: Conditional probability
points: $P(A|B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$ for $P(B)\ne0$ — 'probability of $A$ given $B$ occurred'.
$\text{Multiplication}$: $P(A\cap B)=P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A)$.
$A,B$ are $\text{independent}$ iff $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$; then $P(A|B)=P(A)$ and $P(B|A)=P(B)$.
Independent vs $\text{mutually exclusive}$ are $\text{different}$: mutually exclusive ($P(A\cap B)=0$) with $P(A),P(B)>0$ $\text{cannot be independent}$.
$P(A'|B)=1-P(A|B)$ but $P(A|B')\ne1-P(A|B)$ in general.

notes.heading: Total probability and Bayes
points: If $B_{1},\ldots,B_{n}$ $\text{partition}$ $S$ (mutually exclusive and exhaustive, $P(B_{i})>0$), then for any $A$: $P(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} P(A|B_{i})P(B_{i})$ ($\text{law of total probability}$).
$\text{Bayes' theorem}$: $P(B_{k}|A)=\frac{P(A|B_{k})P(B_{k})}{\sum_{i} P(A|B_{i})P(B_{i})}$ — 'reverse' the conditioning.
Tree diagram: $\text{first level}$ branches are $B_{i}$ with $P(B_{i})$; $\text{second level}$ are $A$ given $B_{i}$.
Bayes is used when you $\text{observe}$ $A$ and want the probability that it came from source $B_{k}$.

notes.heading: Random variable and mean / variance
points: A $\text{random variable}$ $X$ assigns a real number to each outcome in $S$; its $\text{distribution}$ lists $P(X=x_{i})=p_{i}$ with $\sum p_{i}=1$.
$\text{Expectation}$ (mean): $E(X)=\sum x_{i}p_{i}$; $E(X^{2})=\sum x_{i}^{2}p_{i}$.
$\text{Variance}$: $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^{2})-[E(X)]^{2}$; $\text{SD}=\sqrt{\text{Var}}$.
$E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b$; $\text{Var}(aX+b)=a^{2}\text{Var}(X)$ (addition of constant does not change variance).

notes.heading: Bernoulli and Binomial
points: $\text{Bernoulli}$ trial: one trial with $P(\text{success})=p$, $P(\text{failure})=q=1-p$; $E=p$, $\text{Var}=pq$.
$\text{Binomial}$ $X\sim B(n,p)$: $n$ $\text{independent}$ Bernoulli trials; $P(X=r)=C(n,r)p^{r}q^{n-r}$ for $r=0,\ldots,n$.
$\text{Mean}$ $E(X)=np$; $\text{Variance}$ $\text{Var}(X)=npq$; $\text{SD}=\sqrt{npq}$.
$\text{Mode}$ is near $np$; recurrence $\frac{P(r+1)}{P(r)}=\frac{n-r}{r+1}\cdot\frac{p}{q}$ helps find the most probable $r$.
$P(X\ge k)=1-\sum_{r=0}^{k-1} C(n,r)p^{r}q^{n-r}$ — for 'at least' use complement when $k$ is large.

notes.heading: Exam strategy
points: For $\text{Bayes}$ word problems, first list the $\text{partition}$ $B_{i}$ and their priors $P(B_{i})$, then the likelihoods $P(A|B_{i})$.
'At least one success in $n$ trials' $=1-q^{n}$; 'at most one' $=q^{n}+n p q^{n-1}$.
For $\text{expectation}$ without full distribution, use linearity: $E(X+Y)=E(X)+E(Y)$ even when $X,Y$ are not independent.
Check $\text{independence}$ before multiplying: blind $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ without verifying independence is a standard error.

traps: $P(A|B)$ vs $P(B|A)$ — $\text{swapping}$ them is the $\text{Bayes trap}$; denominators differ.
'Independent' does $\text{not}$ mean 'mutually exclusive' — independent requires $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, mutually exclusive means $P(A\cap B)=0$.
In $\text{total probability}$, $B_i$ must $\text{partition}$ $S$ (exhaustive, disjoint) — missing a case makes $P(A)$ wrong.
For binomial, $p$ must be $\text{same}$ in each trial and trials $\text{independent}$ — non-identical $p$ is not binomial.
$\text{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\text{Var}(X)$ — variance $\text{ignores}$ additive constant $b$, but $\text{scales}$ by $a^2$.

notes.heading: Heights & Distances — break into right triangles
points: $\text{Angle of elevation}$ is measured $\text{up}$ from horizontal; $\text{depression}$ is $\text{down}$ — both share the horizontal line.
Draw the $\text{horizontal line}$ at the observer's eye level; the $\text{line of sight}$ makes the given angle with it.
For two positions of observation, draw $\text{two right triangles}$ sharing a common side (height or distance) and write $\tan$ equations.
If the object is on the other side of a river/building, introduce the $\text{unknown distance}$ as $x$ and solve.
Always convert $\text{degrees}$ to a sketch before writing equations — most errors are $\text{wrong triangle}$ selection.

notes.heading: General solution of trig equations
points: $\sin x = \sin\alpha \Rightarrow x = n\pi + (-1)^{n}\alpha$, $n\in Z$; principal $\alpha\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$.
$\cos x = \cos\alpha \Rightarrow x = 2n\pi \pm \alpha$, $\alpha\in[0,\pi]$.
$\tan x = \tan\alpha \Rightarrow x = n\pi + \alpha$, $\alpha\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$; period $\pi$.
For $a\cos x + b\sin x = c$, write as $R\cos(x-\phi)=c$ where $R=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$, $\cos\phi=a/R$, $\sin\phi=b/R$; solution exists only if $|c|\le R$.
To find $\text{number of solutions}$ in $[0,2\pi]$, draw the $\text{graph}$ or use $\text{unit circle}$ — don't just count formulas.

notes.heading: Sine, Cosine, Projection rules
points: $\text{Sine rule}$: $\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}=2R$ where $R$ is $\text{circumradius}$.
$\text{Cosine rule}$: $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\cos A$ (and cyclic).
$\text{Projection rule}$: $a = b\cos C + c\cos B$ (and cyclic) — $\text{the side is sum of projections}$ of the other two.
$\text{Half-angle}$: $\sin\frac{A}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}}$, $\cos\frac{A}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{s(s-a)}{bc}}$, $\tan\frac{A}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{s(s-a)}}$ where $s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$.

notes.heading: Area, circumradius and inradius
points: $\Delta = \frac12 ab\sin C = \frac12 bc\sin A = \frac12 ca\sin B$.
$\text{Heron}$: $\Delta = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$.
$R = \frac{abc}{4\Delta}$; $r = \frac{\Delta}{s}$; $r = 4R\sin\frac{A}{2}\sin\frac{B}{2}\sin\frac{C}{2}$.
$\text{Ex-radii}$: $r_{1}=\frac{\Delta}{s-a}$, $r_{2}=\frac{\Delta}{s-b}$, $r_{3}=\frac{\Delta}{s-c}$; and $r_{1}+r_{2}+r_{3}=4R+r$.
Napier's analogy: $\tan\frac{A-B}{2}=\frac{a-b}{a+b}\cot\frac{C}{2}$ — rarely asked but useful.

notes.heading: Ambiguous case and triangle construction
points: Given $a,b,A$ (SSA), the number of triangles depends on $a$ vs $b\sin A$: if $a<b\sin A$ no triangle, $a=b\sin A$ one right triangle, $b\sin A<a<b$ two triangles, $a\ge b$ one triangle.
$\text{Triangle inequalities}$: $a+b>c$, $b+c>a$, $c+a>b$ — $\text{check before accepting}$ a solution.
If two sides and included angle are given, use $\text{cosine rule}$ to find third side; if two angles and a side, use $\text{sine rule}$.
For $\text{heights}$ word problems, the $\text{ambiguous}$ is not about SSA but about $\text{which side is height}$ — label clearly.

formulas.d: In the right triangle containing the angle.
Compare a with b sin A to count triangles.

traps: In general solution, $\alpha$ must be the $\text{principal value}$ in its defined interval — not any solution.
For $a\cos x+b\sin x=c$, check $|c|\le\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ before solving — otherwise $\text{no solution}$.
Sine rule gives $\text{two possible angles}$ when using $\sin^{-1}$ (since $\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta$) — check $\text{ambiguous case}$.
Heights problems: $\text{distance between two objects}$ is often not the base of the same right triangle — $\text{draw separately}$.
Heron's formula needs $s$ as $\text{semi-perimeter}$, not perimeter — $\text{divide by 2}$.
Don't confuse $r$ (inradius) with $R$ (circumradius): $r=\Delta/s$, $R=abc/4\Delta$.

notes.heading: Statements and logical connectives
points: A $\text{statement}$ is a sentence that is either $\text{true}$ or $\text{false}$, not both; questions, exclamations, and variable expressions like '$x>2$' are $\text{not statements}$ until $x$ is fixed.
$\text{Negation}$ $\sim p$ has opposite truth value to $p$.
$p\wedge q$ ('$p$ and $q$') is true only when $\text{both}$ are true; $p\vee q$ ('$p$ or $q$') is true when $\text{at least one}$ is true.
$\text{Truth table}$ for $\sim$: $T\to F$, $F\to T$; for $\wedge$ only $T\wedge T = T$.

notes.heading: Implications — the most tested
points: $p\to q$ ('if $p$ then $q$') is $\text{false}$ only in the case $p$ true and $q$ false; in all other cases it is $\text{true}$ — this surprises many.
$\text{Converse}$ of $p\to q$ is $q\to p$; $\text{inverse}$ is $\sim p\to\sim q$; $\text{contrapositive}$ is $\sim q\to\sim p$.
$p\to q$ is $\text{logically equivalent}$ to its $\text{contrapositive}$ $\sim q\to\sim p$, but $\text{not}$ to converse or inverse.
$p\leftrightarrow q$ ('$p$ iff $q$') is true when $p$ and $q$ have the $\text{same truth value}$ (both true or both false).
To prove $p\to q$, you may prove $\text{contrapositive}$ $\sim q\to\sim p$ instead — often easier.

notes.heading: Quantifiers
points: $\forall x\,p(x)$ means 'for $\text{all}$ $x$, $p(x)$ is true'; $\exists x\,p(x)$ means 'there $\text{exists}$ an $x$ such that $p(x)$ is true'.
$\sim(\forall x\,p(x)) \equiv \exists x\,\sim p(x)$; $\sim(\exists x\,p(x)) \equiv \forall x\,\sim p(x)$ — $\text{quantifier flips}$ on negation.
'$p$ is $\text{necessary}$ for $q$' means $q\to p$; '$p$ is $\text{sufficient}$ for $q$' means $p\to q$.
An $\text{argument}$ is $\text{valid}$ if the conclusion must be true whenever all premises are true; $\text{check with truth table}$, not intuition.
A $\text{tautology}$ is always true, a $\text{contradiction}$ always false, a $\text{contingency}$ sometimes true.

notes.heading: Mathematical induction — structure
points: $\text{Principle}$: to prove $P(n)$ for all $n\ge1$, show (i) $P(1)$ true (base case) and (ii) $P(k)$ true $\Rightarrow P(k+1)$ true (inductive step).
$\text{Base case}$ may start at $n=0$ or $n=2$ depending on statement — $\text{verify the starting point}$.
$\text{Inductive hypothesis}$ is 'assume $P(k)$ true for some $k\ge1$'; you must $\text{use it}$ to prove $P(k+1)$.
$\text{Strong induction}$: assume $P(1),P(2),\ldots,P(k)$ all true to prove $P(k+1)$ — needed when recurrence uses earlier values.
Typical JEE induction targets: $\text{divisibility}$ ($a^{n}-b^{n}$ divisible by $a-b$), $\text{sums}$ ($\sum_{r=1}^{n} r = n(n+1)/2$), $\text{inequalities}$ ($2^{n}>n^{2}$ for $n\ge5$).

notes.heading: Induction — execution tips
points: For $\text{divisibility}$, write $P(k+1)-P(k)$ to expose the factor; for $a^{k+1}-b^{k+1}$, write $a^{k+1}-b^{k+1}=a(a^{k}-b^{k})+b^{k}(a-b)$.
For $\text{inequalities}$, use the $\text{inductive hypothesis}$ to bound $P(k+1)$ from $P(k)$ and then apply a known inequality like $AM\ge GM$.
Always $\text{state}$ 'by induction, $P(n)$ holds for all $n\ge1$' at the end — the concluding sentence earns the mark.
If the statement is $P(n)$ for $n\ge5$, the base case is $n=5$, not $n=1$.

formulas.d: True when at least one true.
False only when p true, q false.

traps: $p\to q$ is $\text{true}$ when $p$ is $\text{false}$, regardless of $q$ — don't mark it false just because $q$ is false.
Converse and inverse are $\text{not equivalent}$ to the original implication — the contrapositive is.
Negating $\forall$ gives $\exists$ and vice versa — $\text{flip the quantifier}$, not just the statement.
In induction, you must $\text{prove the base case}$ explicitly; assuming $P(k)$ without it is $\text{invalid}$.
For divisibility induction, $\text{factor out}$ $a-b$ correctly — $a^{k+1}-b^{k+1}$ needs the $a(a^{k}-b^{k})$ split, not just $a^{k+1}-b^{k+1}=(a-b)(\cdots)$ circular.

notes.heading: King and Queen — the two most used definite tricks
points: $\text{King}$: $\int_{a}^{b} f(x)dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(a+b-x)dx$ — $\text{replace }x$ by $a+b-x$ and $\text{add}$ the two integrals.
$\text{Queen}$: $\int_{0}^{a} f(x)dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a-x)dx$ (special case with $a=0$).
Strategy: write $I = \int f(x)dx$, also $I = \int f(a+b-x)dx$ by King, then $2I = \int [f(x)+f(a+b-x)]dx$ — often the sum $\text{simplifies dramatically}$ (e.g. $f(x)+f(a+b-x)=1$).
Example: $I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}dx$; King gives $I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}dx$, so $2I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\pi/2$, hence $I=\pi/4$.
$\text{Even/odd}$: $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)dx = 0$ if $f$ odd, $=2\int_{0}^{a} f$ if even — $\text{test }f(-x)$ first.

notes.heading: Wallis and Beta — for $\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^{n}x$
points: Wallis: if $n$ even, $W_{n}=\frac{(n-1)!!}{n!!}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}$; if $n$ odd, $W_{n}=\frac{(n-1)!!}{n!!}$ where $n!!$ is $\text{double factorial}$.
$\text{Beta function}$: $B(p,q)=\int_{0}^{1} x^{p-1}(1-x)^{q-1}dx = \frac{\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)}{\Gamma(p+q)}$; for integer $p,q$, $B(p,q)=\frac{(p-1)!(q-1)!}{(p+q-1)!}$.
Use Beta to evaluate $\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{m}x\cos^{n}x\,dx = \frac12 B\left(\frac{m+1}{2},\frac{n+1}{2}\right)$.
For $\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin^{n}x\,dx$, use symmetry: $=2W_{n}$ when $n$ even? Actually $\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin^{n}x\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{n}x\,dx$ if $n$ even? Check.

notes.heading: Leibniz rule — differentiate a definite integral with variable limits
points: If $F(x)=\int_{a(x)}^{b(x)} f(t)dt$, then $F'(x)=f(b(x))\cdot b'(x) - f(a(x))\cdot a'(x)$ (when $f$ is continuous).
If $F(x)=\int_{a}^{x} f(t)dt$, then $F'(x)=f(x)$ (FTC).
If $F(x)=\int_{0}^{x} f(x-t)g(t)dt$ is a convolution, differentiate via $\text{Leibniz}$ after substituting.
Use Leibniz to find $\text{limits}$ of the form $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1}{x}\int_{0}^{x} f(t)dt = f(0)$.

notes.heading: Bounding integrals without evaluating
points: If $m\le f(x)\le M$ on $[a,b]$, then $m(b-a)\le\int_{a}^{b} f(x)dx\le M(b-a)$ — $\text{estimate}$ the integral.
If $f$ is $\text{monotonic}$, the integral lies between $\text{left Riemann sum}$ and $\text{right sum}$ — useful for $\text{prove existence}$ of root of $F(x)=0$.
For $f(x)\ge0$, $\int_{a}^{b} f(x)dx =0 \Rightarrow f(x)=0$ a.e.; for continuous $f\ge0$, it means $f\equiv0$ on $[a,b]$.
Use $\text{Cauchy-Schwarz}$ for integrals: $\left(\int f g\right)^{2}\le\int f^{2}\cdot\int g^{2}$.

traps: King $+$ Queen need the $\text{new limits}$ to be correctly swapped — $\int_{a}^{b} f(a+b-x)dx$ keeps the same limits $a,b$; don't change them to $b,a$.
Even/odd test is $f(-x)$ vs $f(x)$, not $f(x)$ vs $-f(x)$ after substitution — $\text{plug }-x$ correctly.
Wallis formula needs $n!!$ as $\text{double factorial}$: $5!!=5\cdot3\cdot1$, $6!!=6\cdot4\cdot2$ — don't confuse with $5!$.
Leibniz rule needs $f$ $\text{continuous}$ at the limits; if $f$ has a jump, split the integral.
Bounding an integral with $m\le f\le M$ gives an $\text{estimate}$, not the exact value — don't present it as equality.
